speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I may say in reply to my right hon. friend that I did not attempt any remarks on the second reading because I went rather fully into an explanation of the bill and its merits at the time of introducing the resolution. I also thought that possibly the time of the House would be saved if I waited before going on with the second reading to hear and reply to any criticisms which hon. members might have. I have purposely left the second reading over for a considerable period of time in order that all hon. members of the House might have an opportunity of studying the provisions of the bill carefully. I think it is almost two months since the bill was presented to the House, and in that period of time I have had the privilege of receiving a large number of communications and a large number of deputations in reference to the measure, and I think that both inside and outside of the House there is a pretty general understanding of its main provisions.
I would like to say, however, speaking broadly in reference to the criticisms that have been directed against the bill, that many of them are due to an entire misapprehension of what the government has in mind in the legislation which it has introduced. For example, I notice that many of the newspapers of the country have reported that the government is endeavouring by this legislation to legislate against combines as such, to legislate against the right of manufacturers or merchants to fix a resale price. There is nothing of the kind in the legislation. As a matter of fact, it proceeds from a diametrically opposite point of view. I explained that, I think, pretty fully at the time of introducing the bill. It proceeds broadly on the theory that in this age of commercial and industrial competition, not merely between industry and industry and locality and locality, between the industries of one province and those of another, but between the industries of one countiy and those of another, the industries one might almost say, of one continent and those of another, large combinafMr. Meiehen.l
tions of capital, organizations of business in a large way, are an absolute essential if the business of our country is to hold its own in competition with the business of other countries. But just because it is recognized that it is necessary to have these large organizations of business, so the government recognizes that some restraint must be placed on the possible abuse of great power which may come into their hands. The legislation does not seek in any way to restrict just combinations or agreements between business and industrial houses and firms, but it does seek to protect the public against the possible ill effects of these combinations.
The definition of the word "combine" as related to the provisions of the Act has perhaps occasioned a number of persons that measure of alarm which some of them seem to have had who have not read the definition carefully, and who have thought that the definition goes much further than it does. If the House will look at the definition, and I will draw particular attention to the wording when we are in committee, hon. members will see that the kind of combination referred to is limited to a combination that operates or tends to operate, that has operated or is likely to operate to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, whether consumers, producers or others. No other class of combinations comes within the provisions of this act. If that point is quite clear, I think it will help to remove a good deal of the misconception that has arisen in reference to the legislation. For example, I notice in one press report it was stated that the act did not distinguish between good combines and bad combines. Well, that is the very distinction that is carefully made in the definition itself. Any combination, whether it is in the nature of a trust or merger or the result of some agreement, which is carrying on its business in a reasonable way, not operating to the detriment of the public or against the interest of the public, would not come under the important provisions of this legislation; once, however, it is shown that a combination is so operating as to prejudice the public interest, then that class of combination comes within the provisions of the act, first for purposes of investigation, and secondly, if need be, for purposes of prosecution under the criminal section which has been suggested.
My right hon. friend mentioned that he understood I had a number of amendments to move. I do not know where he got his information; I have one or two very slight amendments which I will mention to the House at the moment. One is to strike out

Combines-Mr. Mackenzie King
in the defining clause the words "in the opinion of the registrar or any commissioner" which appear before the words "have operated or are likely to operate to the detriment of or against the interest of the public." Those words were inserted with reference more particularly to the part of the act which deals with investigation, but when they are read in conjunction with the clause dealing with the new criminal offence which is created by the act, they acquire a significance they were not intended to have, and it is therefore my intention to move when we get into committee thaf those words be stricken out.
I might mention that some of the deputations that have waited on the government have pointed out that perhaps the act was too broad in permitting any individual to lay a complaint before the registrar, and it was suggested that possibly the language of the old Combines Investigation Act which required six persons to unite in presenting a request for an investigation would be a proper safeguard, and that those persons should be restricted, as they were in the old act, to British subjects. I think that is a perfectly proper amendment to have made in the act, and I shall move that also as an amendment when the House goes into committee.
There is one other slight amendment which is to strike out the words "or documents" that appear in section 18, line 42, of the act. The section as drafted makes it obligatory upon any person to give evidence before a registrar or commissioner and to produce documents. It goes on to state, however, that whoever gives testimony cannot be bound in a court of law by the oral testimony so given. The clause as it now reads goes beyond granting protection as respects oral testimony and includes documents. The effect, of the bill as drafted would be that where any incriminatory documents might be disclosed in the case of an investigation, subsequently, when court proceedings were held, a combine might find its means of escape from the just penalty of its illegal actions, by having these documents protected. It is, therefore my purpose to meet such a possible situation by providing that the words "or documents" shall be deleted.
I think, Mr. Speaker, I exp'ained, when introducing the measure in the House, the need for this particular legislation at this time. There is no legislation on the statutes of Canada to-day protecting the great body of consumers or producers against the possible ill-effects of combinations carrying their powers to too great an extreme in the way of monopolizing control of commodities, of unduly enhancing the prices of commodities or restricting their sale in a manner detrimental to the public. The legislation of 1910, the old Combines Investigation Act, was repealed by the legislation of 1919, the Combines and Fair Prices Act and the Board of Commerce Act. The Board of Commerce, as the House knows, did not function as it was expected to function. That legislation has ceased to be of any value, and it is proposed by this enactment to repeal what has become valueless. However, one of the effects of the legislation of 1919 was to make it impossible for section 498 of the Criminal Code to be operative except at the instance of the Board of Commerce. No prosecution could be commenced, under section 498 of the Criminal Code, against a combination in restraint of trade, except at the instance of the Boa'd of Commerce, but as the Board of Commerce is no longer in existence at the present time, even such protection as the law afforded under the Criminal Code is not granted to consumers against the possible ill-effects of these combinations.
Recently there has been a decision given in Ontario, in the case of the Attorney General of the province vs the Wholesale Grocers, which, in the minds of some, would seem to raise a question as to the intra vires of the legislation [DOT] which I have referred to as constituting a part of the Criminal Code. Anticipating that the matter might be referred to in discussion to-day, I asked the Department of Justice for an opinion and I may as well read at this moment the opinion I have received which will answer any questions on that particular point. Mr. Newcombe, Deputy Minister of Justice, stales:
I have considered the judgments of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Ontario in the case of Attorney Genaral vs Canadian Wholesale Grocers, herewith, with relation to its effect as to section 498 of the Criminal Code, and I find that it does not conclude any question as to the authority of parliament to enact that section.
The court was composed of the Chief Justice, Hod-gins. Ferguson and Magee, JJ. The Chief Justice reluctantly considered that he was bound by the observations of Lord Haldane in the Board of Commerce case to hold that section 498 was ultra vires, as not relating to criminal law within the meaning of that section of the British North America Act, 1867. Hodgins and Ferguson, JJ. however, expressly refrained from expressing any opinion against the validity of section 498, although they agreed with the Chief Justice for other reasons that the appeal should be dismissed. Magee, J. concurred in the result without any observations or reasons, and so it stands that the invalidity of section 498 rests only upon the opinion of the Chief Justice.
I do not think that it is at present necessary or advisable that our course of action should be in any wise modified by reason of the view which the Chief

Combines-Mr. Mackenzie King
Justice expressed. I do not think that the question is governed by Lord Haldane's observations, and when it arises for decision we will have an opportunity to make good our claim for legislative authority. Meantime I would proceed upon the assumption that the enactment is intra vires.
Has the question of the authority of parliament to pass this particular bill been placed before the Justice department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. I may say to my hon. friend that this particular measure has been carefully reviewed by the Department of Justice and I am informed that in the opinion of the department it is intra vires.
In regard to this legislation-just by way of helping to make clear the main divisions of it-I may say that the measure falls broadly into two parts. The first part has to do with investigations and the necessary machinery for purposes of investigation. It is intended to provide that where there are grounds for believing that a combine is operating to the detriment of the public, or likely so to operate, any six persons who are British subjects-as it stands now, any individual- may apply to the registrar for an investigation. The registrar will be an officer appointed by the government whose duty it will be to see, in the first instance, whether the evidence that is submitted appears on the face of it to be sufficient to give reasonable grounds for believing that the combination that is alleged is of a character which in the public interest should be investigated. If the registrar comes to the conclusion that the combination is of that character, then he may continue an investigation or may recommend *-or the government of its own initiative may appoint-a commissioner, with the powers which are given to commissioners under the Inquiries Act, to make a full investigation, to satisfy himself, or the commissioners to satisfy themselves, as to whether or not the operation of the alleged combine is against the interest of the public. Judging from past experience it would appear that it is on the whole better that these preliminary investigations should be held in private rather than in public. The purpose of the legislation is not to subject industry and commerce to all kinds of inquisitorial proceedings which may have a baneful or harmful effect, but rather to do as little in the way of interfering with legitimate business and business methods as possible. The bill accordingly provides that so far as this investigation by the commissioners is concerned it shall be held in private,' leaving it, however, to the discretion of the minister-having refMr. Mackenzie King.)
gard to certain contingencies that might arise that theretofore are unforeseen-to say whether any part of the investigation should be public, or whether the report of the investigation should be made public. Up to that point there is nothing in the nature of any criminal proceedings against the combination. However, upon report of a commissioner authority is given to the government to remit or to reduce duties so as to permit of a wider measure of competition, should it appear that the effect of the combination is to take undue advantage of some clause in the tariff. If . it be an unfair advantage of some patent right that is taken, the government, through the Minister of Justice, may proceed for a revocation of the patent right.
Possibly I can best explain what is fundamental in the measure by saying, that in regard to combinations operating to the detriment of the public the belief of the government is that there are certain classes of evils which publicity will do more to remedy than even penalty. In regard to combinations that are actually operating to the detriment of the public, the great difficulty has always been to ascertain just the nature and full extent of their operations. Once that is ascertained, if they are operating to the detriment of the public, and the fact is known, it is natural to expect that the public will speedily find some means to protect itself. Another principle that I think will help to illustrate what is fundamental in this legislation is summed up in the words that private rights cease when they become public wrongs. In other words, the bill does not in any way seek to restrain private individuals in the making of any contracts or agreements, tacit or implied or open, which they may wish to make, so long as in the exercise of their private rights they do not carry matters to a point where their joint action becomes ar public wrong in the form of a combination operating to the detriment of the public.
I think these few preliminary remarks will serve sufficiently for an introduction of a consideration in committee of the provisions of the bill.

Before going into committee I would like to present a case to the minister and ask him if it would come under the combine's bill which we have now before us. The newspapers have recently informed us that there is a daily newspaper combine in Canada. We have been told that an effort was made to establish a new daily paper in the city of Ottawa. If our information is correct, it was a newspaper that was proposed to dis-

Combines-Mr. Hocken
seminate the doctrines of the Liberal party. But the executive of the daily newspapers association voted almost unanimously that the necessary service to carry on such a paper should be denied the man who wanted to establish a newspaper in Ottawa. To help the Prime Minister to a conclusion, if it is an improper thing for a man taking any manufactured article and fix the price, or to enter into a combine with others in the same line of manufacture in disposing of his goods to the public, is it not a much more serious matter when public opinion is stifled, and the opportunity to present to the public of this country, or this city or any city, a particular aspect of the affairs of the country, is refused, and that the men who have the money and are willing to put it up for this purpose shall be denied the privilege of doing it. I cannot conceive, Mr. Speaker, of any more dangerous form of combine than a newspaper combine. If you carry this out, the same organization of a dozen men, forming the executive of the daily newspaper association, can determine just where a newspaper shall be printed, and where one shall not be printed. If a company should be organized to establish a new evening paper, say in the city of Toronto, that company would have to go to the men who form the executive of the daily newspaper associations of Canada and ask their permission.
Why?

Not to ask their permission to put in a plant and print some kind ot newspaper, but to ask their permission to get the service absolutely essential to the production of a newspaper that will sell. And at the same time, Mr. Speaker, this government subsidizes, to the extent of $50,000 a year a telegraphic service for the use of the daily newspapers; and the group of men who happen for the time to form this association have it in their hands to prevent a man here or there or anywhere from enlightening the public as he thinks the public ought to be enlightened. Will the Prime Minister tell us in view of what he has said, whether this bill will apply to such a case? Because he has said that this bill is designed to control these men and prevent an abuse of the great power that might come into their hands. A very great power rests in the hands of daily newspaper editors and proprietors; practically everybody in Canada reads the newspapers nowadays, and there is no class or group of men in Canada who exercise more power than the men
who are conducting the daily newspapers of the country.
And also the weekly papers?

Also the weekly papers, but the weekly comes out once a week, the daily six times a week. The one will have a circulation of 20,000 or 30,000 and the other 150,OOC. I do not renege on my statement that the men who exercise the greatest power in the public interest in Canada are the men who control the great newspapers. And unless there is opportunity given to those who think they have a message-it may be a political or it may be a social message-to publish that message for the benefit of the public, and if they are not allowed to give that message to the public on account of restrictions imposed by their competitors, I think it may be safely said that these competitors are prejudicing tne' public interest, to use the words of the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister further said that there were many classes of offences, combines, perhaps, where publicity would do more to effect a remedy than would a penalty. I entirely agree with that statement. I think publicity is one of the greatest penalties that some men can suffer for their misdeeds. If you have all the newspapers in the hands of a few, so that all kinds of abuses might exist and not have any publicity, then the public interest is surely most seriously prejudiced. If the Prime Minister feels so disposed, will he answer the question as to whether he would not consider a daily newspaper combine as one that would come within this act.

Before the right hon. Prime Minister answers the question, I would remind the House that we are not yet at the committee stage, and therefore if the right hon. member speaks now it closes the debate, according to rule 21, unless by leave of the House the minister replies to the pertinent question put by the hon. member.
I desire to speak on the second reading, but the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) desires to ask the Prime Minister this question before he takes his seat, if it may be put in that way.
Perhaps the right hon. premier would prefer to answer all these questions when he exercises his right of reply, under rule 21 of the rules of debate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the question asked by the hon. member illustrates perhaps as well as anything could, the merits of the proceedings we are proposing to establish by this legislation in dealing with the kind of case he has cited. My hon. friend says that if you have all the newspapers in the hands of a few, you have one of the worst combines conceivable. I agree absolutely with that. I think there could be no more fatal combination, so far as the public is concerned, than that all the news of the country should be controlled by a few men, in such a way as to make it impossible for any others to enter the field of news competition. However, in regard to the case just cited,- the application which has been made by the Liberal party for a paper in this city,-the contention on the part of those who refused to give the right to permit a new paper to acquire certain news is that they think the public interest is being best served by the papers that are here at the present time. They contend that there is not a monopoly. They contend that another newspaper can come in and start to-morrow on its own account, if the parties wish. However, they have among themselves, as I understand it, an agreement as respects the sale of a certain class of news that is acquired, by cable or telegram. It is that particular class of news which they refuse to give to any other paper. Whether that refusal amounts to a monopoly of a character which is injurious to the public, is something that, I think, can be determined only as a result of an investigation. This legislation provides that where there is prima facie ground for believing that a combine exists which is operating in a manner detrimental to the public, then any six persons may apply to a registrar for an investigation. Taking the case in point, I would assume that any registrar appointed under this legislation would feel, it if were possible to cite evidence of the character to which my hon. friend has made reference, that he should immediately investigate and see how far that monopoly, or alleged monopoly, extended in its operation, whether it went the length of shdtting out other papers from this city, or whether its effort was merely to deny to a paper coming into a field a certain class of news which it either could or could not acquire in some other way. If there were reasonable grounds for believing that the public was being injured as a consequence of this monopoly, an investigation would then be made by a com-
missioner. The commissioner would take all the evidence under oath; he would then give a statement to the public, and the public would be in a position to judge whether or not the combination was of that serious character which some might be inclined to believe it to be. I doubt if anyone could pronounce upon the merits of the particular case without having all the facts of the case before him. That is why this legislation proceeds in two stages: The first setting forth the means of getting the fullest information and giving publicity to that information; the second stage providing a remedy whereby, if need be by way of criminal prosecution, any action of the combination which is against the public interest may be effectively put a stop to.

Mr. Speaker, I quite realise that appearing as an apologist in any sense for anything that might be called a combine lays one open to attack and possible misinterpretation of one's position. During the past twenty years there has been a steady growth in the intense organization of business, in the formation of what is commonly known as combines, in the bringing of businesses of a similar character under the control of a smaller executive head, thus lowering costs of operation, increas-
4 p.m. ing efficiency and, in many cases, stabilizing both production and prices. This tendency has been met on the part of the public in different ways; but there has been, with certain sections of the public, a growing resentment-shall I say?-against what is commonly known as a combine, without, perhaps, any careful defining of what a combine is. I notice that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in introducing this legislation, both on a former occasion and today, stressed particularly that the object of the legislation and the objective, I might say, that he had in mind was to interfere, not with what might be termed legitimate combines, but only with such as were likely to operate detrimentally to the public interest. Further I noticed that he said that at the present time there was no legislation by which the government could properly deal with circumstances arising out of, perhaps, an abuse of privilege or power on the part of large combinations of business. It is from that angle that I desire to examine this legislation. I may say that I took advantage of the advice the Prime Minister gave, when he introduced this legislation, to give it careful study, and as a layman I rather hesitate to enter into what might appear to be somewhat of a legal argument, because I claim no right or no particular ability to do so. I have examined it as

Combines-Mr. Stevens
a layman, I might say as an accountant, because that is my profession. I have examined it with care and with, perhaps, some right to pass an opinion after careful study. I want to examine it before the House as it appeals to me, with reasonable brevity and at the same time with a desire to impress upon the House in particular one or two points which, in my estimation, characterise this legislation, and warrant me at least in opposing it.
The crux of the whole bill is to be found in the interpretation clause, clause 2-in the description or interpretation there set forth of what a combine is in the eyes of this legislation. I intend, by the way, to divide this into three or four heads and to deal with them very briefly as I proceed. I want first to make as clear a presentation of the facts as I can, and later on I purpose arguing the points. In the first place, clause 2 defines a combine as being one of such business organizations as
-have operated or are likely to operate to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, whether consumers, producers or others.
I ask the House to bear that word "others" in mind, and let us examine it briefly. Who are "others"? Let us assume that a group of businesses find it desirable to combine, think 'it is in their interest and in the interest of their business that they Should combine. They do so. Some of them may not enter the combine. It easily may, and very often does, result that the combined businesses operate at a lower cost, give better service, are more efficient and stabilized, and because of that they undersell the so-called independent firms or firms that stand out. These are "others" who are injured by the combination, although the public may be distinctly benefited. In this I am not drawing a bow at venture, but I am describing what has happened time and again during the past twenty-five years. Under this legislation as it now stands, such a combine, such a combination, is declared to be an offensive institution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but he has used words which indicate that the class of combination referred to' would not come under the legislation at all. If what he says is true, namely, that a certain combination would really operate to the benefit of the public, that would put it out of the class referred to in the definition.

I do not wish to be impertinent to the Prime Minister; but if he will wait a moment. I purpose showing that
that is precisely what the legislation does	not say.	As	regards this	particular portion of the definition, I submit that	two words	in	it prevent the	veryobject to which the Prime Minister refers. For instance, the registrar must interpret this. If a combination operates to the detriment of consumers, producers or others-and "others" is not defined in any limited sense-then under this bill it is a combination that is detrimental to the public. And furthermore, the word "likely" introduced there gives a very wide scope for interpretation solely by the registrar; that is,	the	registrar is the	solejudge	whether or	not	this combination is
likely at some future time to be detrimental to the public interest.
But that is not all upon which I rest my argument. I take the next portion of the interpretation clause. It further describes "combine" to include:	.
[DOT]-the relation resulting from purchase, lease or acquisition by any person of any control over or interest in the whole or part of the business of any other person.
How is that clause likely to operate? Supposing we have a group of, say, A. B. C and D. If A acquires a portion or the whole of the business of B and as a result of that combination C and D suffer, then under this bill the registrar must find that this is a combination to the detriment of consumers, producers "or others," as is set forth earlier in this clause.
Then it also deals with any agreement, etc., "designed to fix a common price of re-sale." This is a very vital point. This covers any agreement or undertaking between a manufacturer and a sales agency whereby the price of resale is fixed. Under this proposed legislation such an institution would be declared by the registrar to be detrimental to the public interest. Let us look at this for a moment. We know, at least I am pretty fully persuaded of it myself, that many manufacturers of this and other countries, enjoying the highest possible standing with the public, fix the price of their goods. The price is printed on the label or stamped upon the article itself, and the article is sold from one end of the country to the other by all dealers at that fixed price. The result is to stabilize its distribution and to maintain a price at a reasonable figure to prevent the avaricious retailer or agency taking advantage of a shortage at any particular time and exacting a higher price for it. I was shown the other day a statement by the Ford Motor Company which very carefully and fully illustrates this. . They point out that they have all along fixed the price of their cars and parts to all their
Combines-Mr. Stevens

sales agencies, and these agencies not only sell the article at this fixed price but give certain services in addition. I think everybody here who drives a Ford car knows what splendid service the Ford agencies render. I do not drive a Ford car so I have not had the advantage of this thorough service. These agencies sell on a commission of 20 per cent. This may seem high, but it is pointed out that it includes service. The net result of it all has been that during the last few years the Ford car has actually dropped in price until to-day it is selling for about $100 less than in 1914. That is merely one illustration; there are scores one might give of how the fixing of the resale price by a manufacturer usually, and I might say generally, is in the interest of the public; and yet under this proposed legislation this practice would be demed a combine detrimental to the interests of the public.
Then-and this is of particular interest not only to manufacturers but tc others-this clause describes a combine as one which enters into an agreement for
-lessening competition in, or substantially controlling manufacture, purchase, barter, sale, storage, transportation, insurance or supply.
I can bring forward several illustrations of what may happen under such a provision. I shall give these briefly because the moment I mention them the facts will be present in the minds of my hon. friends. Take, for instance, dairies. In Ottawa there is the Ottawa Dairy. I think they have some competition now, but for many years they were without any competition, and yet I recall that at the time the cost of living investigation was held by a parliamentary committee in 1919 it was shown beyond all peradventure that the Ottawa Dairy, while a distinct monopoly under this clause, did operate in the interest of the public. My right hon. friend will answer all this I know by saying, "Then it does not come under this measure." But the registrar is forced to so interpret under this clause. The clause to which I am now referring is an undertaking or an agreement or a contract substantially controlling competition and the purchase, sale, etc., of an article. In the city of Vancouver there is another illustration of what might happen under this measure, for if it were in force the Producers' Dairy would be Challenged. This company, organized and owned by the producers of milk in the Fraser valley, in other words, by the dairy farmers, supplies milk [DOT] to the public at a moderate price; yet they were challenged by the independent dealers. Under this bill that daily company could be

effectively challenged, and in my estimation the registrar would be bound t.o declare it to be a combination detrimental to the interests of the public, or to the "producers, consumers or others." Then we have the formation of a wheat pool, which would be for the purpose of eliminating competition-in the wording here, for the purpose of "controlling the purchase, barter, sale, storage, transportation." After listening, as we have, for several years to the disclosures of the difficulties and extra costs now imposed by the present system, no one will question that if another system could be worked out it would be in the interests of the public; and yet if it were done it would, as I have said, come under this clause, and the registrar, if he were appealed to, would have to declare it to be detrimental to the public interest. Then again take the Fruit Union of the Okanagan. There, perhaps, you have a more striking illustration than anywhere else of an organization deliberately formed for the purpose of controlling the price and distribution of their products; and yet, under this clause, it would be a combine. I merely give these illustrations to bring home to the House the significance of this interpretation clause.
Now I turn to what is my chief criticism of the bill, that in effect it declares to be a crime that which is, without question, ordinary, sound business sense. 1 have already intimated that, during the past twenty-five years in particular, there has been a growing tendency for business to get together to eliminate useless competition. By that I mean vicious competition-not competition in service, but competition which simply seeks to slay a competitor. There has been an endeavour to eliminate useless competition and to build up associations of kindred businesses, thus reducing overhead and executive charges, improving the efficiency of distribution and stabilizing both prices and production. Without such combinations there is a tendency to over-production during periods of prosperity, with recurring periods of depression and under-production. This is one of the greatest problems facing economists to-day. It is cropping up everywhere. It has cropped up in the Agricultural Conditions committee in the Banking and Commerce committee. In the consideration of any of the great problems of the day this question is the most perplexing one that arises. Yet through the medium of many of the large combinations of business in this country that evil has been, I will not say elminated, but reduced, and the stabilization of both production and

Combines-Mr. Stevens
distribution has been secured. Now, why should we seek to erect that into a crime?- for that is what parliament, in effect, does, and it is the feature of the bill above all others that I object to. I believe, Sir, that this bill is raised upon false premises. Any given action is not a crime simply because parliament may choose so to describe it; it must in itself be a criminal act. The judgment to which the right hon. Prime Minister has referred is filled with extracts from decisions of the Privy Council and of eminent jurists throughout the Empire, not only in the case of the Board of Commerce, not only in the case of the Wholesale Grocers of Ontario, bnt in the case of Austrialia vs. the Adelaide Steamship Company and many others. It is set forth most clearly that merely to declare, through the Criminal Code, a thing to be a crime does not necessarily make it a crime- and that is what I particularly wish to emphasize to-day. The act of combination is not an offence. The act of combination and the most rigid advantage taken of it is not an offence. But if a group of business men or others-and this applies or ought to apply to all classes alike-deliberately conspire to injure competitors; if the object of the getting together is to effect injury to others, then you have an offence, then you have a crime. On the other hand, where the combination or the getting together is purely to promote the interests, if you like, of those combining, there is no crime and there should not be said to be a crime; because, as I have stated, and as I intend to insist, the country at large usually benefits from such combinations.
Reference has been made to section 49S of the Criminal Code, and I want to deal with that aspect of the question for a moment, because I regard it as very interesting and very important. It is true that Chief Justice Meredith does in his decision question section 498 of the Criminal Code is intra vires of parliament. I am not as able to discuss or elucidate the point as others here who have legal training, but I hope that what I say will lead them to a closer examination of the whole question. In that decision and in the decisions of the Privy Council it is emphasized that section 498 of the Criminal Code was inserted to give this parliament jurisdiction. Let me put it a little differently. Parliament has jurisdiction over criminal matters, but not over property and civil rights, the latter belonging to the provinces. Parliament declares, through the criminal code and in words very similar to the interpretation that I have read, that "it is an
indictable offence" and so on, against those who "conspire, combine, agree or arrange with other persons," and so on, "to unduly limit transportation facilities" and so forth-similar language to that contained in this bill. It is the erecting of the combination into a crime that the Privy Council and Chief Justice Meredith object to. They do not say that the conspiracy should not be legislated against in the criminal code. Let parliament make such provision in the criminal code that it can deal with deliberate conspiracies for the restraint of trade, and so forth; let them make it perfectly clear that it is the conspiracy they are after-then I think parliament will have rendered good service to the public. I submit to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), as I would to the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) if he were in his seat, that careful examination of this bill will show that its adoption would place the government in virtually the same position that the Board of Commerce Act, that section 498 of the Criminal Code, is in to-day-without relieving, without changing or improving the condition throughout the country.
Then, the bill is inquisitorial in its character. It gives very wide powers to registrars. The Prime Minister has pointed out that under the provisions of the bill certain investigations will be held by one nominated as a registrar. This is a preliminary investigation to enable the registrar to declare whether or not the combination complained of is a combine under the terms of this act. He carries on his inquisition or his inquiry secretly; in other words, it is a star chamber proceeding. I appeal again to the good sense of this House; if there is one thing more than another that is necessary to subdue unreasonable combinations, it is publicity, not secrecy. In the second place, I submit that any bona fide business that has not been carried on with any intent to injure others should not be subjected to a secret or any other kind of inquiry. The only business that should be interfered with, harassed, inquired into, is a' business that has committed some offence, a combination that is wrong. My right hon. friend pointed out, laying some emphasis upon it-and he made the same statement before a very large body of citizens who waited upon him a few weeks ago-that unless a combination had done wrong they need fear nothing under this act. But he is asking parliament to give to the registrar powers beyond those of the courts of this land; he is enabling the registrar to inquire secretly into any business or any concern complained of. Why, there would be no difficulty at any time, anywhere, day or night, summer or winter, to

Combines-Mr. Stevens

get six citizens of Canada to complain against some institution. I do not say ignorant people, but uninformed people, are very prone to complain of businesses or institutions wherever they may be. Six uninformed, irresponsible individuals may ask for an investigation. The registrar proceeds to investigate. He calls for all documents, contracts, books and so forth of the company. He can step into the office, examine into prices, obtain any information he demands. All that he asks for must be produced; the concern which is the subject of inquiry has no recourse but to give up everything that is demanded pertaining to the secrets of its business. I submit that one rival desiring to get information regarding another rival's business, perhaps more successful than his own, perhaps underselling him on the market, would find it the simplest thing in the world to get that information through such an institution as this.
That is where private investigation comes in.

Not only is the registrar or prosecutor not sworn to secrecy, but the minister or the registrar or the commissioner -it is so set forth in the bill-may disclose any part or all of the findings. I want my hon. friend to note that. I object to this private investigation, I am absolutely opposed to it. The registrar or a commissioner has the absolute right to determine the portion or the whole of the investigation to be disclosed, and to whom it can be disclosed. If one person desires to obtain the sgcrets of his competitor and stands in well with the commissioner, if he has pull-shall we say?- with the registrar or the minister, he can get a copy of the results of the investigation and no one need be the wiser. I submit that no such power, no such privilege, should be given to any one, two or three persons.
Let me turn to another phase of the bill. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister has said, and I expected him to say it, that under this bill he is taking certain powers; in clause 23 and clause 24, I think it is. Those powers are as follows: If a combination or a concern seems to be taking advantage of the tariff to unduly enhance prices, under this bill the Prime Minister says, the Governor in Council may for the time being place such an article on the free list. He has all that power now, and I wish the House would follow me in this particular. Not only in regard to this, but as I have already pointed out in the Criminal Code we have almost the identical power set forth in this bill, with but slight amendments to make them conform to the 
judgment of the Privy Council and the Supreme Court of Ontario. Under the Inquiries Act we can make the inquiries where it is considered to be in the interests of Canada and of law and order to do so. But in the Customs Tariff, section 12, I find a clause that is almost identical with the one inserted in this bill. Let me read it so that parliament may be seized of the powers already invested in the government. Section 12 of the Customs Tariff reads as follows, beginning at subsection 2:
2.	Whenever the Governor in Council deems it to be in the public interest to inquire into any conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement alleged to exist among manufacturers or dealers in any article of commerce to unduly promote the advantage of the manufacturers or dealers in such article at the expense of the consumers, the Governor in Council may commission or empower any judge of the Supreme Court, or of the Exchequer Court of Canada, or of any superior court or county court In Canada, to hold an inquiry in a summary way and report, to the Governor in Council whether such conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement exists.
3.	The judge may compel the attendance of witnesses and examine them under oath and require the production of books and papers, and shall have such other necessary powers as are conferred upon him by the Governor in Council for the purpose of such inquiry.
4.	If the judge reports that such conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement exists in repect of such article, the Governor in Council may admit the article free of duty, or so reduce the duty thereon as to give to the public the benefit of reasonable competition in the article, if it appears to the Governor in Council that such disadvantage to the consumer is facilitated by the duties of customs imposed on a like article.
There is absolute power to deal with this matter-no need whatever of this legislation. Furthermore, I will say this to the Prime Minister: If this legislation were to pass and it were found desirable to admit some article free, unquestionably his Minister of Justice would invoke section 12 of the Customs Tariff and not the clause in this bill.
I would point out another difference. In this bill before us it is proposed to entrust all this very, very wide power to whom? To a registrar or a commissioner. In the customs tariff it provides that the government may empower a judge of the various courts- an infinitely fairer, an infinitely better method of deciding an important point of that kind-and at the same time it preserves the rights of the person so inquired into.
The next point referred to by the Prime Minister was the revocation of a patent if it was found that by the use of that patent an abuse existed. I would again bring to his attention that during this session we have passed a Patent Act, and in that act at great length and in detail we provided against all of that. It is there. So parliament ought to.

Combines-Mr. Carroll
be seized of this: In the Criminal Code, in the Inquiries Act, in the Customs Tariff Act, and in the Patent Act all of the powers asked for in this bill are now fixed, and fixed in the proper place, fixed in a manner that protects and will protect the interests of the public.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I desire to sum up very briefly what I have said, not to weary the House with further detail. I oppose the bill: First, because a combine is usually prompted by efforts for efficiency and economy, and generally results in better service, the stabilizing of prices and the uniformity of supply. Second, because for persons or corporations to combine for mutual benefit is not in itself a crime nor should it be so declared either by inference or specifically. Third, the crime of conspiring, to injure other persons or to interfere with trade should be dealt with under the criminal code, and if the code as it is now drafted is not exactly fitting to the case sections 496 and 498 should be amended so as to fit.
My further objection is that the bill is inquisitorial. It will, if enforced, harass business without serving any useful purpose, and if ever there was a time when business should be free from interference and from that type of inquiry that simply disturbs and harasses it, that time is now. I venture to say that business of all kinds throughout the length and breadth of this country is struggling under the burden of taxation, under the burden of laws that really are going back, as it were, to the Middle Ages, and this would only be an added burden to the carrying on of business.
All that is sought for in this bill is much better provided for in the Criminal Code, the Inquiries Act, the Patent Act and the Customs Act. These acts with slight amendments constitute the proper medium of treatment and provide all the needed machinery, so that this bill merely duplicates powers, confuses jurisdiction, and multiplies public cost without adding one whit to the public protection.
Lastly, assuming the object of the bill to be the exposure of criminal interference with trade, profiteering and the conservation of the public rights, I submit, Sir, that no such end will be attained under this bill. On the contrary it impedes and harasses legitimate business development, it will victimize the innocent, and at the same time it opens innumerable avenues of escape for the guilty. In that regard I again remind the House that similar legislation to this has been repeatedly declared ultra vires of this parliament by the Privy Council and is called in question by this important judgment of Chief
wn
Justice Meredith. Therefore, why should we invite further litigation to determine this point when we can escape all that by, as I have already mentioned, insisting upon the real offence, namely, the conspiracy feature, and dealing with it under the Criminal Code.
Mr. W. F. CARR,OLL (Cape Breton South and Richmond): I believe this legislation is intra vires of this parliament and that no better legislation has been introduced here for half a century. The present bill is primarily and mainly, I think, for the protection of the consumers of Canada and it is from that aspect that I am going to discuss the subject. Various efforts have been made in the past to bring within reach of the law, persons who combine to enhance the prices of the necessities of life, but I do not think any of that legislation has been effective. In the past, in enacting laws against combines and monopolies, parliament did not take power to see that the law was enforced, and that persons wTho violated its provisions were penalized. The buck was passed to the legislatures and to the attorney generals of the provinces, and the Dominion statute contained no provision for making the law effective. In 1919 there was an attempt to legislate on this matter, but it was not of a nature at all akin to the present measure, and I believe our courts have declared that certain parts of that statute are ultra vires of this parliament. The Prime Minister this afternoon, in answer to my question, gave us the assurance that in the opinion of the Department of Justice the present bill was intra vires of this parliament; I am going to take it for granted that such is the case until the highest tribunal in the land has declared to the contrary.
I am in perfect accord with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) when he states that all combines are not bad, and that combinations of business interests in this country have done a great deal to benefit not only the producers and the consumers but the nation as a whole. Combinations of capital have done much to lessen the cost of certain articles which are among the necessaries of life in Canada, and to that extent the combination of capital is a splendid thing. But when capital combines to enhance the price of the necessaries of life, when it combines to take the last cent out of the consumers of Canada, then I say that such a combination should be declared a crime by this parliament, and I want to congratulate the government on bringing down legislation with that object in view. My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) I think, is somewhat astray in con-
Combines-Mr. Carroll

eluding that all combines would be declared criminal under this bill. It has no such intention. The interpretation clause says-

I did not say that they would all be declared criminal. I said that in view of the interpretation clause the registrars would be forced to declare them combines, which is all that the bill does. The bill does not deal with the criminal feature of it at all.
But the registrar would not be forced to- declare these associations as combines.
Yes.

At any rate, he would not be forced to investigate a concern which is not a combine within the meaning of the bili. As a preliminary the registrar will take means to assure himself that the concern is not such a combine as the bill has in view. For example, if six persons go to the registrar with a complaint, he may demand of the business firm or company concerned the right to look over its books in private. That is a proviso with which I am strictly in accord. The manager of the firm shows his books to the registrar, and I am presuming that neither .his government, nor any other government which may be in power in Canada, will appoint registrars who are not honest and honourable. Now, the registrar will go to the managers of this business firm and ask them, in a quiet manner, to produce their books. Then I feel assured that if it is not a combine, such as this bill intends chasing and hounding to death-and I hope that course will be pursued-the managers will be very -glad to produce their books when the registrar in the course of a few hours can inform himself whether the concern is such a combine as comes within the four corners of the proposed statute. This procedure ought to cover the objection taken by my hon. friend. But the hon. member can refer to the interpretation clause and what will he find? He will find this:
(a) The expression "combine" in this act shall be deemed to have reference to such combines immediately hereinafter defined as in the opinion of the registrar or any commissioner have operated or are likely to operate to the detriment of or against the interest of the public-
And so on. The whole of these provisions must be read together. It is not necessary to show, for example, that there is a merger or a monopoly in order to bring that concern within the provisions of the act; that merger or combine or monopoly must be operating to

the detriment of the public. My hon. friend has fallen down in his argument by ignoring that provision of the legislation.
What public?

I need not tell my hon. friend for St. John and Albert that "public" is a very well-defined expression. Further down in the clause there is included in the definition the limiting of facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing in any commodity. But they must be doing this and operating against the public weal in doing it. In all these cases you must go back to section (a) of the act before coming to a conclusion that a trust, a monopoly, or a combine, or a transportation business, is a combine within the act, which this bill declares a combine.

The hon. member should
in his argument, in all fairness, read the words "whether consumer, producer or others" which qualifies this provision.

The hon. member is getting away from the argument I am presenting. However I will come to the question the hon. member has asked. I do not know exactly what significance that word "others" has. I will be quite frank with the hon. member, because I think in this country we are either consumers or producers, and as a matter of fact we are all consumers.

consumer.

That is very clever,
no doubt. That is one of the cleverest things I have heard from the hon. member in his whole career in this parliament, and I have heard him say a good many things. My hon. friend for Vancouver Centre has seriously argued that, if there were a small concern in Hamiltion, engaged, say, in the manufacture of ploughs, it was right, just and equitable that another large concern in that city should combine, or should try by any underhand means or met! od, to put that small concern out of business? The hon. member is stating my own argument. I argued that if, by conspiracy or underhand means, such a thing as that were done it should be punished under the Criminal Code, but if it were done by competition, as it might be done under this act, there would be no crime.
No crime?
No offence.

The hon. member must know that this parliament is absolutely supreme in making crime. They can make almost any action of man a crime if they so desire.
Now my hon. friend talks about the privacies of the investigation by the registrar, and says those privacies are wrong. In another instance he calls them star chamber methods of doing business. I want to say to my hon. friend that I believe after the registrar has gone to the institution and made a personal investigation of the documents and so on, any further investigation should be of a public character. That far I agree with the hon. member. I am in hopes that the registrars will be men of such calibre that, having made a personal investigation on the premises, as they are allowed to do by this bill, and finding no evidence which will make the concern investigated a criminal under the act, there will be no further inquiry. I believe that all further investigations should be of an absolutely public nature and that the public should have
access to them. My hon. friend for Vancouver Centre says that he has read the bill. He is a serious student when he takes up any question and his studies are serious, as everyone in the House knows, but I think he is mistaken or misled when he attempts to show the House that the registrar is all-powerful in so far as the whole situation is concerned. What are the facts? The registrar investigates. There may be counsel for the government and counsel for the combine which is being investigated. The evidence is taken, and the court has all the functions and powers of a court excepting that it does not pass sentence. My hon. friend and the House must not forget the fact that the registrar has no authority to come to a conclusion. He passes the matter on to the minister, and the minister decides if tnere is sumeient evidence to have the person, firm or corporation indicted under the Criminal Code. If the minister thinks there is sufficient evidence, he so advises the attorney general of the province, and the attorney general, while there can be no pressure brought to bear upon him to draw an indictment or lay information, may bring an indictment before the court, and the person, if person it be, or corporation, if corporation it be, accused of the crime, has the same rights before that criminal court as any other citizen of Canada. The accused may go before a jury or may elect to have a speedy trial be-for the county or district court judge. If the attorney general does not see fit to proceed with the investigation, charge or trial, the solicitor general, within six months, may, off his own bat, proceed to bring home to those people their crime.
I do not think my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre wished to mislead the House, but I want to show that this registrar has nothing in the world to do, except to make a fair investigation, to pass the papers, so to speak, to the minister who has charge of the matter, and if the minister is of opinion there is something to investigate he passes the case on to the attorney general. If the attorney general does not act, the solicitor general may proceed with the case and lay a charge. My hon. friend says that all the cures for the present situation in Canada are to be found within two or three statutes and he mentions them. He mentions section 12 of the Tariff Act, he mentioned the Patent Act and the Criminal Code. If my hon. friend will read section 497-

-he will find an allo-gether different state of affairs from that which
