appears in this particular section. For example, take first the procedure. There is nothing in the Criminal Code which makes it incumbent upon this parliament or this government or any future government to prosecute offences under that act. The whole thing is left in the hands of the attorney general of the province. Under this bill we have the machinery which will surely ensure at some time, even though it be late, an investigation into a combine or conspiracy in restraint of trade. When we talk about conspiracy in restraint of trade, do hon. members in this House believe it is restraint of trade for example, if several wholesale dealers get together with the retailers in the various places where they are selling their goods, and say "Here we have a corner on something. We have a corner, in this particular vicinity, in potatoes, any kind of vegetables, any necessity of life. We are, it is true, getting a big profit now, but we are going to extract 10 per cent more from the pockets of the consumers." Is that a restraint of trade? I say, it is not a restraint of trade, and those sections of the code do not touch dealers who may act in that way. That is one of the things that the consumers of this country are concerned with, namely, that there is a conspiracy, if you will, but not a conspiracy in restraint of trade-you cannot call it that- between the wholesalers and retailers of this country to maintain prices.
Does the hon. membeer think such an act would be permitted under paragraph (c) of section 498 of the code?

I doubt if it could be
reached by that section.
If it could not, it certainly could not under this legislation.
That is an opinion.
There is no doubt about it.

I doubt very much if it could. It is, however, to the procedure that I am referring in the present instance. There is no doubt in the world to-day that there must be conspiracies to keep up prices of certain commodities in this country. There is no doubt that such conspiracies have existed in the past, and if this legislation is properly enforced, it will be a very great blessing to the great mass of the consumers of this country-and we are all consumers.
My hon. friend speaks about the remedies that are supplied in this legislation, having an existence already, for example, under the
{Mr. Carroll.)
Patent Act. I do not know that we can have in this country too many remedies against a man who, having secured a patent, misuses it to the detriment of the public. While I have not had time to go into the clause of the Patent Act dealing with this, I would say, notwithstanding that fact, that it is necessary to have this particular item incorporated also in this legislation, enforced as it will be by the government of Canada.
My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) speaks of the powers of the Tariff Act. I did not even have time to read section 12, I think it is, of the Tariff Act but if my hon. friend will look over it again, he will find that there is a good deal of distinction. While in the Tariff Act the bodies and persons who make an inquiry are mentioned, this is adding another body to inquire under that act it is adding a body which, I think, can make the inquiry much moie readily than can a judge of the Exchequer Court or the Supreme Court. My hon. friend is not a lawyer, but I am sure he knows something of the delays which surround courts of law in various actions which may be brought before them. In this case we have a simple method of investigating ; and if there are trusts and combines, which are doing things which are to the detriment of the people of this country, another method of bringing them to justice is not going to hurt any person, but it is certainly going to help the consuming masses, if the law reaches out to persons who are taking the last cent unduly, and, as the bill says, to the detriment of the public.
My hon. friend had also something to say regarding property and civil rights. It is true that the legislatures of our provinces have what we may call absolute jurisdiction over property and civil rights. That, however, has its limitations. If this parliament undertakes to deal with something within its
5 p.m. authority and, by chance, encroaches upon property and civil rights in a province, then this parliament has the right to pass that legislation. That is the consensus of opinion which one may gather from reading opinions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in connection with this matter. But we are not so much concerned in this case with property and civil rights as we are with trade and commerce, and the matter of trade and commerce comes foursquare within the authority of this parliament. It is trade and commerce specifically at which this legislation is aimed, and if it encroaches, to some extent, upon the matter of property and civil rights in a province, yet this par-

Combines-Mr. Evans
liament has absolute power to pass such a measure. While I do not put myself as a lawyer on the same plane as the Deputy Minister of Justice, I think he is absolutely right in his opinion expressed, to the government, that this government has power to pass the legislation in question.
I did not intend taking up so much of the time of the House in connection with this matter. I have some criticisms to make of this bill, and as I said, one of them is the criticism which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre made. That criticism is as to the public nature of the inquiry, the court inquiry held by the court registrar or commissioner, not the private inquiry which he may make into a man's business by going to his house, or shop, or store. Again, the minister should not have the last say on this question. The minister has the last say whether or not, in his opinion, sufficient information has come out of the registrar s investigation to entitle him to ask the attorney-general of a province to prosecute. From the minister's decision in that matter there is no appeal as the act is at present constituted. I would suggest that there might be an appeal to the Governor in Council, because two heads are better than one. For instance, the minister having control of this measure may or may not be a lawyer. He may not know what weight should be given to certain evidence. In his particular position in life, he may not be trained to know exactly what certain evidence means. If the Minister of Justice is not the minister referred to in the context of this bill, there should be an appeal to or a consideration, if one is asked, by either the Minister of Justice or members of the government as a whole. I have received various communications from people, not only from my part of the country, but as far west as the home of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, and they are all of one opinion, that if this legislation is properly administered, it will be a great blessing to the people of Canada who do not have large bank accounts, in other words, the masses of the consuming public. Two or three investigations, and two or three indictments brought in against people who are active in a propaganda to extract every cent possible out of the consumers, will waken the big business people of this country to a sense of duty and responsibility, and they will not, in future, do things which will cost them in the vicinity of S20,000 or $25,000.

This bill proposes to deal with one of the most important matters that has come before parliament this session, particularly in its relation to the everyday commodities that the people have to buy, and it is from this viewpoint that I wish to discuss the bill.
The history of combines in Canada, is the history of the tariff-one evil has been produced by the other. Oil refining was protected by the tariff and was controlled by a ring as early as 1879. Mr. John Charlton, then a member of this House, said that "tariffs were bound to breed combines," and no prophecy concerning the National Policy has ever proved more true. He cautioned the House then that the tariff would speedily bring monopolies, trusts and mergers into existence, and that they would not be easily broken up. He said it would take more than one verdict of the people, more than one general election, to loosen the deathlike grip which these monopolies, trusts and mergers would fasten on the people of this country.
Well, combines, trusts and mergers did develop. Since Mr. Charlton's warning, legislation has been repeatedly enacted by parliament, ostensibly to check the rapacity of these organizations. There was a measure of this kind passed in 1889, another in 1897, still another in 1907, and the last in 1910-all to no purpose. At the election of 1896 our free trade party got into power; the original National Policy party-or as I like to term it, the trade restriction party-of that time was overthrown and in its place came a professedly free trade party. For fifteen years this free trade party held power, but the trusts, combines and mergers gained daily in monopolistic control of every commodity, and to-day these predatory organizations are more securely in control in every particular than they ever were before. I say in every particular because there never was a time when the manufacturing and distributing of all the commodities the people use were so completely dominated by classes of men, many of whom should never be in possession of the power which they exercise to-day, keeping, according to their way of putting it, the trade of the country in the proper channels. The trusts to-day have more complete control in this country than in any other in the world, including the United States, where these combinations first originated. I assert there can be no dislodgement of these monopolistic organizations, nor any effective control over them, so long as our present protective tariff
Combines-Mr, Evans

with all its amendments stands on our statute books, or while there continues to be the same community of interest between the politicians of business and the politicians who sit in this House.
Now, this evil has gone on unchecked ever since Sir John A. Macdonald in 1878 in a speech at Hamilton told the manufacturers he would try to meet their wishes if they would tell him what they needed. He was leader of the opposition at that time and of course was not able to invite the manufacturers to council at Ottawa. But this he did on his return to office, and since that time the manufacturers and others who form combinations for their own benefit have had plain sailing at the expense of the consumers, notwithstanding all the anti-combine legislation that has been enacted and the successive changes of government,
In 1881 the cotton manufacturers, who for two years previously had received increased privileges from the government, met together and organized a complete union and at once agreed to advance their prices. Prior to this combination the industry had been paying "only" about 30 per cent in dividends; since then some of these cotton concerns have paid very much higher dividends. All kinds of industries, large and small, were soon organized with the same end in view-enhancement of prices. By 1889 they were so numerous and aggressive that there were complaints in parliament about the way consumers were being victimized. Indeed, one Liberal member who drew attention to this new development declared that the interests of these combines and the government supporters were so closely linked together that the government would be hampered in dealing with the evil. At that time one combine in Toronto actually put up for sale among its members the privilege of tendering, without competition, for the supply of coal to the Dominion and Ontario governments.
It was plain to both parties that these combines were brought into being by the protective tariff, so to offset the agitation against trade restriction an act was passed by the Macdonald government for the suppression of combinations in restraint of trade. Obviously the politicians responsible for that act in 18S9 never intended it to be anything more than a mere make-believe for there could be no conceivable reason for the manufao* turers dickering with the politicians for a high protective tariff when an effective measure on the statute books would have prevented them taking full advantage of such a tariff. Now I predict the government will

have hard work to persuade the people that this bill is ever intended to do anything more than were the bills of their predecessors. Nc combines were broken up by the act of 1889. In 1897 too the Liberal government, then newly elected, anxious to appear before the country as desiring to carry out some of its pre-election pledges according to the 1893 platform, enacted sitll another anti-combine law. There was performed in this House at that time perhaps the greatest farce that was ever staged in the Dominion. The Conservative party, then in opposition, feigned to be frightened by the bill, and well did they play their part. Sir Charles Tupper declared it to be legislation of the most vicious kind and that it was undemocratic in that it gave the minister or the council too much power. But both the government and the opposition knew that the bill was the greatest political joke ever played on the people. The Liberal government had no intention of seriously assailing any trust or combine, indeed they never had after the conference with the delegation of manufacturers on June 18th, 1890, shortly before the general election.
Now, they added this anti-combine legislation to the Tariff Act, but they made no provision for its enforcement by any officer of the Dominion government. After it had been in force for some thirteen years, there was, be it said to its credit, one case-just one solitary instance-of a reduction in the tariff because of proceedings against a combination in restraint of trade. But it cost the concern that laid the information 81,800 to prove its charge; and I never knew of a subsequent case. As evidence, too, of the hold that the protected combines were exercising over the Dominion legislators, I have only to point out that the screws were tightened on the consumers of this land at different'tariff revisions, 1884 and 1894, when heavier import penalities were imposed on the consumers while the free list began to swell for the manufacturers. This destroyed, I think, all argument in favour of the tariff as a means of creating employment or of creating a home market. After all, it is in the years from 1900 to 1914 that we must look for the greatest development of the trusts and combines as well as the ineffective attempts to obviate the evils that this development brought with it. The act assented to in 1910, known as the Combines Investigation Act, proved useless, as did its predecessors; the process was too unwieldy.
The legislation now proposed would seem to be effective in that it makes it a criminal offence for any person to assist knowingly or be privy to combines operating to the public

Combines-Mr. Evans
harm. I see there is also a registrar to be appointed who shall be the chief officer through whom proceedings may be instituted. But even this will not avail, as I will show. Whether combines or agreements in restraint of trade flourish in this country to the detriment of the public may admit of some argument. But I am wondering where the Prime Minister means to begin in connection with this bill, since all the business of the country, whether financial or industrial, or, particularly, relating to the distribution of all goods, is operated or controlled' by combines, mergers and trusts. These control the manufacture, distribution and prices of everything the public need to use, and there is no getting away from under their lash as long as the tariff, with its anti-dumping provisions and its latest amendments, stands on the statute book as it does to-day.
The Prime Minister would be well advised to withdraw this bill and at the same time abolish some of the existing legislation that hands power to the combines, trusts and mergers, For instance, the dumping clause as it stands to-day delivers the consumers over to the combines to do as they please with them. It is impossible now for an importer to know what duty he will have to pay. I know of one case where a retailer who last year bought goods in the United States and paid the duty on their entering this country was assessed under the anti-dumping clause for an additional amount because he was not a jobber or a wholesaler. A considerable quantity of his goods was retailed out before the antidumping law* was applied to him-it makes a difference who the importer is. As if this were not enough, an amendment was made to the Customs Tariff Act in the closing days of the last session giving the minister complete power to place any price he likes on any natural products that enter too keenly into competition with any Canadian concern. That amendment completely delivered the consumers of this land into the hands of the jobbers, the wholesalers, and the retailers; the provision was made entirely in their interests. The anti-dumping act has closed Up the trading activities, so far as agricultural implements are concerned, of one of the greatest co-operative companies that was ever formed in the Dominion. The anti-dumping act as it stands to-day with its amendments is a piece of galley slave legislation. It is impossible under it for a co-operative company to import anything for distribution in a cooperative way, because no co-operative company is recognized as a jobber and it is required to pay duty, not on the invoice price
of the manufacturer, but on the retailer's price. In fact, the minister can do as he likes, and I say as long as these provisions are on our statute books, any anti-combine legislation we can bring in of the nature of this bill will be futile.
The anti-dumping law is legislation that with one stroke forms into one great combine every distributing concern in the country- and the government asks us to believe that it can introduce legislation that will tend to lower the cost of living and to control combines. I, for one, cannot believe it. I do not think there is any sincerity in this matter, when the present tariff system is left entirely untouched-the very legislation that gives the combines all the power they need. If there is one thing more than another that this country needs to-day it is that people shall have freedom to purchase their commodities where they please. But there has sprung up between the producers and the consumers a combine whose rules are absolute, a combine which is recognized under the law of this land, which is recognized by the tariff system of this country, because in the Tariff Act the words "value for home consumption" are interpreted according to whom the importer happens to be. That is, only a jobber is allowed to import on the invoice price of the manufacturer. If a consumer or a co-operative company, distributing in a co-operative way, imports, the words "value for home consumption" are interpreted to mean the retail price in the country of origin, which is an injustice. Under such conditions, Sir, this proposed bill can give no relief; any investigation is bound to prove fruitless. The Customs Act is interpreted in favour of those who still hold the lives of the people in bondage through high prices.
Now, clause 7 of the bill enacts that the minister himself shall decide whether or not an investigation shall be proceeded with. The decision of the minister is final. There can be no appeal or review. So the same minister who is now interpreting the antidumping clause in the interest, as I have shown, of the trusts and combines is to decide whether or not an investigation shall be made at all, and his decision is not subject to appeal or review. If this government with the help of the opposition put through, as it did on June 22 last, an amendment to the Tariff Act that closed up the very last gap of liberty to the consumers of this land, I ask what credence will the electors give to the government in the enactment of this proposed bill? I say that this proposed bill can give no relief under such conditions. The Customs Act is
Combines-Mr. Evans

interpreted in favour of those who still have the power. Take that amendment of June 22 last. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr.Fielding) declared in his original budget speech that this anti-dumping amendment was to be left out as it was an unnecessary interference with trade. Just what pressure from the politicians of business was brought to bear on the present cabinet between that time and June 22 last when the Minister of Customs moved his amendment, I do not know; but there is a chance now for the whole Liberal party to free itself from all suspicion by doing something tangible, something that will give the people themselves the power to deal with these trusts and mergers in a way that will be effective.

Mr. Speaker, I rise not for the purpose of urging violent opposition to the spirit of the bill as now brought down, because I am quite satisfied in my own mind, in fact I am certain, that the peopla of Canada are quite satisfied that the Prime Minister would bring down no legislation that was not imbued with a spirit of equity and right.
Oh, oh.
I hear some hon. gentlemen jeer. However, that is my opinion, and it is the opinion of the rest of Canada.
What is the evidence?
Everything.

It has increased very largely since the time my right hon. friend is alluding to. However, I did rise for the purpose of stating that I do not think that the manner in which this bill is worded does carry out the spirit in which it is brought down. The bill is intended to aim at trusts, combines and mergers which are unfair or injurious to trade. I read the bill in quite the contrary light as aimed at practically all combines, trusts and mergers, whether they be fair or whether they be unfair. That, I am perfectly sure, is not the spirit in which the bill has been brought down to the House at the present time.
The history of this bill has been explained briefly not only on its first reading but also again to-day, and what that history really comes down to is this: that the Combines and Fair Prices Act, which is more or less dependent on the Board of Commerce Act, not having functioned properly, and repealing, as it does, the Combines Investigation Act of 1910, the only actual legislation in force at the present time on the subject is Article 498

of the Criminal Code. In the explanation on the first reading of this bill it was stated that some effective machinery was necessary so that Article 498 of the Criminal Code could be put into effect for the purpose of the investigation of combines, mergers, and such like, and the punishment of those who may have been involved therein. That, I take it, is the necessity for the bill at the present time.
I am quite aware that on a motion for the second reading of the bill now before the House is not the proper time or place to urge amendments, but I do wish to urge on the government and on the Prime Minister in particular this fact, that the business world in parts of Canada is very much concerned over the bill as brought down, and I think that it will stand very careful scrutiny and very careful study, not with the object of not having it put on the statute book in the spirit in which it is intended t(5 be placed there, but rather with the object of eliminating certain objectionable features which at the present time business interests think are very deleterious to their interests. I want to make it perfectly clear to every hon. gentleman in the House that in speaking to this bill I do [DOT] not defend for a single moment any combine, any trust, any merger or any agreement of any kind or description which is injurious to trade, which is unfair or burdensome to the public. Let me make that perfectly clear in the most emphatic language that I can use with politeness in this assembly; let there be no mistake about it. But I also desire to state in equally emphatic language, in the most emphatic language I can use, that I do not think legislation should be placed on the statute book at the present time which will brand combines, business agreements, mergers, trusts and business arrangements of that description as combines in the unfair sense in which that word is used; in other words, I do not think that business agreements as they exist at the present time should be called unfair combines unless first of all they are proved to be unfair. If we immediately start out and state that every combine is unfair, every business interest, every trust unfair-I know that the bill does not intend to Bay that- but if we start out presupposing that, the business community will never know for a moment where they are.
Probably if there is any further debate on the bill at the present time the cost of living will be urged as being attributable to combines, trusts and mergers. I think I am right in saying that the public mind has for many

years associated the high cost of living with the existence of combines, trusts and mergers so-called. I do not think that that is quite right. Perhaps in a few isolated cases a trust or combine may increase the cost of an article of commerce, but on the whole I do not think that is the case.
You do not agree then with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) ?
I have not heard the Minister of Labour speak this afternoon.
Have you read any of his speeches in the last campaign?

"I have not seen so great faith, no, not in Israel."

My right hon. friend would be exceedingly fortunate if such great faith existed on his side as exists on this.
I was going on to state when I was interrupted that I do not think that combines, mergers and trusts so-called have increased materially the cost of living, because when one comes to think of it a combine, trust or merger of various interests more or less spells efficiency, more or less brings about the cheapening of production, and bringing about the cheapening of production brings about the fact that more labour can be employed. I read with a great deal of pleasure the speech which the Prime Minister made when Minister of Labour in 1910 when that act was brought into effect. I see my hon. friend the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) smiling; my statement apparently gives him a great deal of pleasure. I think, perhaps, it would do my hon. friend much good if he read the speech over again and became imbued -with its spirit.
Sir HENRY" DRAYTON: I am afraid the hon. gentleman cannot give me the credit for the smile, it came from my left.

I apologize to my hon. friend. I see that he is not prejudiced against what I am advising him to read. However, at that time the Prime Minister spoke as follows:
Similarly while combines and trusts may have, had the effect in some cases of increasing prices, they have
not always had that effect but sometimes an effect entirely different, and I would like the House to understand that in introducing this legislation no attempt is being made to legislate against combines, mergers, and trusts as such.
Later on in the same address he stated:
Another point I would like to make clear is that trusts and combines may not be injurious, that in some respects they may be profitable. That is a point that has been raised. This legislation is in no way aimed against trusts, combines and mergers as such, but rather only at the possible wrongful use or abuse of their power, of which certain of these combinations may be guilty.
I have not the slightest doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the present bill, as brought down, fully intends to carry out and fully intends to emphasize what the Prime Minister said twelve years ago as regards combines and mergers. But the point I desire to bring before the House is this: I do not think that the bill as drafted and brought down does carry out that spirit in effect. Part of the legislation which has been spoken about to-day is section 498 of the Criminal Code. Anyone reading that section can come to but one conclusion and that conclusion will be this, namely, there must be wrong intent in the making and the prosecution of any combine. In other words the wrong animus must be pre-existent before a combine is inquired into and called an unfair combine. Now, I claim that section 2 of the present bill does not clearly show that a combine has to be unfair, that its animus has to be incorrect before it is investigated. The words of this section are certainly very broad, and I do think that qualification of the section should be made before a business, or a merger, or a trust can be called a combine. In other words it should be made clear beyond peradventure that the animus of the combine itself is wrongful before an investigation takes place. I do not think the wording of that section, as I have said, is very clear.
Now, we must all freely admit in this House that in business life there are combines, there are mergers, there are trusts, there is fixing of prices, there are trade agreements. All these things must exist in commerce. Commerce could not go ahead unless there were such agreements. The manufacturer would never know where he was, the producer would never know where he was, the consumer would never know where he was either. These trusts, mergers and combines- providing the animus behind them is correct -should be allowed to go on unheeded and not be inquired into. Because, as a matter of fact as business affairs now stand business is only on the up grade. Every investigation that is made impedes business, every return
Combines-Mr. Marler

that a business house has to make simply increases the cost of production. Business is already overtaxed and I claim, Mr. Speaker, that business at the present time-in so far as it is possible to do so, in so far as it is possible in fairness and equity to the public- should not be disturbed by further investigations unless those investigations are essential, unless those investigations are necessary, unless the animus is first of all determined to be wrong. In other words, I believe that before any investigation is made wrong doing or wrong intention should be proved on the part of that business.
Approaching nearer to the words of' the bill it does appear to me that it has been framed in such a way as to call for action on the part of someone who was absolutely fair-minded in every way, who understood industrial disputes, and who was imbued with a spirit of honesty and right. Under the provisions of the bill six people can come forward and demand an investigation. I will come to that question again later on but what I want to make clear at the present time is this: Six people can come and demand an investigation. Now, if everybody in this country of ours was imbued with a spirit of fairness there would be no question to be raised at all. But unfortunately, and I think I must say this, I do not think that the mentality generally-I am speaking of the mentality not in the way of a sense of mind but an attitude generally-of people towards business affairs, towards large business, is the same as it was many years ago. There is without doubt a spirit abroad of more or less jealousy of success, a desire more or less to pull down when it is seen that a business has been successful by reason of operating it for many years in a fair and equitable manner. I fear, Mr. Speaker, that that spirit is abroad. That spirit did not exist before the war in exactly the same manner as it exists to-day-I must say that. I find the attitude of many people in business affairs appears to be very much different. Although it is true, I might say in passing, that the war was supposed to purify us, that the war was fought for democracy and to make the world safe, I have not yet been able to find where that purification or that desire for democracy in order to make the world safe comes in, although it should have come in on account of the suffering that took place and the service that was rendered during the struggle. What I say is that there is an unnecessary carping criticism of successful business methods in Canada at the present time. Bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that I admit where a trust is injurious and is shown' to be in- #
jurious a business merger is wrong. The point I desire to convey is that where a business has been successful by hard and honest work there is a distinct carping criticism of it. I will say this further: Almost from time immemorial in the ways of commercial and business * life there have been, agreements. These agreements have been recognized and have continued to be recognized. Nevertheless the spirit is abroad at the present time, I take it, that would think nothing whatever of tearing down a business that had been properly built up, of tearing down an agreement that had been in force for very many years.
No doubt this act was carefully prepared, and I believe that in bringing down this act the government has no intention whatsoever of trying to destroy any business of that description. It has one intention and one desire, a perfectly proper desire-to cause investigations of trusts, mergers and agreements which are injurious, unfair and burdensome to the public. It is the desire of the government that those agreements should be investigated and put a stop to and that those responsible for su,ch conditions should be punished. That 1 say is perfectly right, but at the same time I do not think that a business which has gone ahead in a fair, honest, equitable way in the face of the whole community should be touched or investigated or subjected to more inconvenience than business is subjected to at the present time-because the more business is disturbed, the greater is the cost of carrying it on and the slower will be the process of reconstruction which our country so much needs at the present time. The more business is disturbed the more does the lack of stability get abroad in this country, and if there is anything we want it is stability, m order that we may progress in our ordinary business lives.
Now, Mr. Speaker I would like to take up in a very brief form the bill itself, and to discuss, as I understand them, certain provisions as they appear in it, and the procedure which is involved. The first step is the complaint, and the second is the preliminary investigation to find out if an actual investigation should or should not take place. The third step is the actual investigation and the fourth step is the subsequent action by the Attorney General or the Solicitor General as the case may be. I wil take up each of those steps very briefly.
The first is the complaint as provided for under section 5 of the bill, subject to the amendments which the Prime Minister has suggested to-day. That is to say, instead of "any one person resident in Canada," the act

Combines-Mr. Marler
will be amended more or less along the lines of the 1910 act; so as to provide for investigation on the complaint of six or more persons, British subjects, resident in Canada, of full age, and so on. That I admit is a distinct improvement to the section in the bill as it stands now. But can we, in fairness, Mr. Speaker, place any business in the hands of any six people in this country? Can we not at any time get together six people who would make a complaint about any business, and who would cause an investigation to be then and there made? If the section, which is the crux of the whole bill in defining a combine distinctly stated that the only combines and the only trusts or mergers which were affected were trusts, combines or mergers which, either prima facie or by some reasonable means were shown to be injurious to trade or burdensome to the public, then the present objection that I am urging might be quite unfounded, but as the bill now stands it means-and it.can only mean one thing- that six people taken from any part of Canada can demand an investigation at any time of any business at all which they think is a combine or a restriction of trade. It does not make any difference what the business is, it does not make any difference what the registrar thinks, it does not make any difference *what a commissioner under the act thinks, or what the government or anybody else may think-those six people, can bring about an investigation by doing what, Mr. Speaker? All they have to do is to file an application under section 5 of the act, and the application states in general terms simply the name and address of the applicants, the nature of the alleged combine, and the manner in which and the possible extent to which the alleged combine is believed to operate against the public. Now it does not take anyone with a very high degree of skill to conjecture up in his own mind any difficulties at all, in order to have any six of these people lay a complaint of that description.
I say again, Sir, that I do think there should be sufficient qualification in this act, in some manner or of some description, and I repeat particularly to the government and Prime Minister that I do not criticize the spirit of the act at all, but I do criticize the machinery and the wording. I say that that clause should be amended in such a way as to provide that those six people whoever they may be, should show more reasonable or just cause of facts before they can, by a mere writing, by a mere declaration placed in the hands of the registrar, say that this business or that is a combine, and that this business or that should be investigated. It is all very well for
six people, under a solemn act of parliament, to stand Up and say that my business or anyone else's business is a combine. That is a stigma, it is not a name that any respectable business expects to be called, because the word "combine" is not used in the ordinary sense of the term, but as something which is unfair and unjust. Here we have likely to be placed on the statute book- I hope it will not be placed there-a section which will give six people the right to state that any business is a combine.
There is another point Mr. Speaker, which comes up under this section of the act, and no doubt the government has considered it to some extent. Does the government realize how many demands, or how may allegations, or how many so called applications they will have under an act of this description? I venture to say, Sir, in the conditions which are in existence at the present time in this country, and which I have alluded to, that there will be thousands of applications under this act. I believe that six people who are discontented and jealous of some other man's business will say "That man is making too much money, let us tear his business up, let us have it investigated and see if a combine exists or not." It is not an unnatural thing for six people who are not endowed with all the pleasures or the money that they would like in this world, perhaps finding themselves very pinched, to be more or less jealous of success, because they are are not as fortunate as others. I do not think I would blame them, and I do not think anyone would blame them. But here is the provision of the act and here is what it means, that six people can get together, and at any time ask for an investigation of this alleged combine. I believe the government will find, under this act which is being brought down in its present terms today, that they will have, not hundreds but thousands of investigations on their hands which they never expected for a moment.
Has the registrar not to declare that he is satisfied with the application?

I was coming to that point. It was my next point. Perhaps if it is not discourteous to my hon. friend I will answer that after recess.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock, I was defining the
Combines-Mr. Mdrier

procedure to be effected under the bill relating to the investigation of combines. I had previously stated that in accordance with the procedure laid down in the bill, there were apparently four steps. The first was the complaint. The second was the preliminary inquiry in order to ascertain if a more detailed investigation was required. The third was the detailed investigation under which a finding or no finding was made as the case might be. The fourth step was the prosecution under the offence as so committed, at the instance or with the assistance of the Attorney General or Solicitor General, as the case might be. I had taken up the first of these steps, namely the complaint, as set out in clause 5 of the bill, and I had defined at some length the reasons why I thought clause 5 of the bill did not actually convey the intention the government had in bringing this bill down. It is not necessary at the present time to repeat or to recapitulate the remarks which I made before the House rose.
I will, therefore, pass on to the second step, namely, preliminary inquiry which the registrar is required to make after the laying of the information, or more properly speaking, the laying of the complaint under clause 5 of the bill itself. Clause 6 of the bill is imperative, it is not permissive. In other words, when a complaint is laid by the six persons as they are designated in the amendment suggested by the Prime Minister to the bill in question, the registrar shall then and there cause an inquiry to be made into the alleged combine or alleged restraint of trade, or any of the other causes set out in the definition of a combine under clause 2 of the bill. As I say, that action of the registrar is imperative on the complaint being laid. It is optional for the registrar to make a preliminary investigation, if he thinks fit, even without a complaint being laid. If he believes a combination exists, he may then and there go ahead and make the investigation himself. It is quite true under the succeeding clause-clause 7 of the bill-if the registrar finds that the complaint is frivolous or vexatious, no actual, definite inquiry takes place. In other words, possibly no offence would be found under this legislation. The point I desire to make now is this, that an investigation or a preliminary investigation must, in any event, take place in order that the registrar may ascertain whether the allegations made by the applicants in their complaint are or are not well founded, because, without making that investigation into the business, merger, trust, call it what you will, it will be utterly impossible for the

registrar to say whether the complaint is frivolous or vexatious or not.
Would an investigation into the books of a company or combine at its office be sufficient?

I think very likely it would be quite sufficient. I was coming to that just in a moment. As I say, the registrar would be required to make that investigation. The point I made in my remarks this afternoon, was that I thought if there was no title, or no evidence, or, in fact, nothing to show whether an actual combine existed in a particular business or trust, that business or trust, as the case might be, should be left severely alone. In other words, because six people complain and file documentary evidence-and this is only documentary evidence -under clause 5 of this particular bill, I do not think that business should be immediately stigmatized as a combine, in secret, it is quite true, perhaps not in public, nor that it should, as it would, be put to the expense and annoyance of an examination, it will therefore mean that any business is subjected to an inquiry of a more .or less searching character on the complaint being made.
Now, why should not something like the following procedure be adopted? Why should not these six selfsame camplainants be called before the registrar and asked to state their case as to the existence of the alleged combine? Then if the proofs which they propose to adduce are considered sufficient by the registrar to justify an investigation it could be proceeded with. I do not claim that no investigation should be made, but I do think that the condition precedent to making even a preliminary investigation should be the production of evidence in proper form by the complainants to show that wrong has been done, and thereupon such wrong can be righted in due course. As the bill stands at present the mere production of documentary evidence alone, without any questioning of the complainants at all, leaves no option to the registrar but to conduct an examination of the business complained of. I humbly suggest to the government that the acceptance of my suggestion would cure a good deal of what at present appears defective in this particular section.
As I have said, the registrar must make an investigation to determine even if the complaint is frivolous or vexatious. That provision, I think, so far as is practicable, should be absolutely removed from the bill. In other words, even at the risk of repetition, I do think just cause should be

Combines-Mr. Marler
shown against any known combine, merger or business, call it what you will, before the preliminary investigation takes place at all. Of course, if upon investigation the complaint is found to be frivolous or vexatious it is dismissed; there is nothing more to be said about it. But if the complaint is found not to be frivolous or vexatious, subject to the qualifications I have already referred to, there is no reason why a thorough inquiry should not be made. That brings me to the next step-the actual inquiry.
This brings me back to section 14 of the bill. There are various other sections relating to the same subject but it is not necessary for me to take them in detail at present because we are only speaking in general terms and I am sure that any suggestions made to the government in the interim will receive careful consideration. But the bill clearly stresses what I think is a consistent element of publicity. It is true that the registrar may or may not conduct the preliminary investigation in private; but he may make it in public, and I do think that publicity should be avoided until it is found there is just cause for investigation. If after the complaint is laid an examination of the six complainants discloses that there is reasonable grounds for a preliminary inquiry, then by all means proceed with that preliminary inquiry; but do not let any part of such inquiry be conducted in public until the registrar finds there is just cause of complaint against the alleged merger or combine in restraint of trade. 1 would respectfully suggest to the government that the bill be made imperative in that regard-that there be no publicity during the preliminary inquiry. I cannot state this point in too emphatic terms. What would happen if this was hot made definite in the bill? A complaint might be made against a business, and whether such complaint was good or bad the preliminary investigation would mean a tremendous amount of publicity which many a business could ill afford to be the subject of. Therefore I repeat, Sir, that this section should be amended so as to make it imperative that the preliminary inquiry be conducted in private until it is found that a searching investigation is justified.
Another section of the bill to which I wish to draw attention is No. 34, which reads as follows:
Nothing in this act shall be construed to apply to combinations of workmen or employees for their own reasonable protection as such workmen or employees.
In any remarks I have to make with respect to this section I wish it to be abundantly clear to every hon. member that I see no possible objections to combinations of workmen and
employees for their reasonable protection. I for one believe that labour should be given its just rights precisely in the same way as capital is given its just rights. After all, there are practically three elements, I take it, in the relations between capital and labour: capital, labour and the community itself. All are interdependent one on the other, each must be given its reasonable and just rights. But why is it necessary in this bill to exclude the operation of its provisions against combinations of workmen or employees. I do not believe that any combination of workmen or employees would ask to be excluded from the operation of this bill. I cannot for a moment conceive that any labour body would be afraid of having its organization investigated. Therefore I do not see why labour organizations should not be included in this bill the same as any business organization, and I would ask the government to take this point under consideration also.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have spoken at some length as regards this bill, and I have stressed several points, the principal being these, and I will not detain the House very long in recapitulating what I have said. I do think that section 2 is not sufficiently distinct; in other words, I think the section should be made so abundantly clear that no combine or merger which is not actually operating in restraint of trade or in any other way doing wrong should be subject to inquiry at all.
My second point is that the bill as a whole should recognize that there must be combines, trusts and mergers and agreements, and that it is not these combinations or these agreements that are wrong, it is the animus which is behind them. In other words, if there is wrong behind any of these agreements, let the wrong be investigated; but the animus should be proved to be wrong before the investigation is ordered. I stressed that, Mr. Speaker, to some considerable extent.
My third point was in regard to the way in which a complaint may be laid. I suggested there that six persons could possibly lay many complaints and that the government might have a great deal of difficulty in looking into all the complaints which might be made under this bill, and I do believe that many more complaints would be made than the government has any idea of.
The fourth point I raised was that the complaint should first be examined into, that the complainants should be called before the registrar and their evidence examined before any inquiry was instituted.
My fifth was that the preliminary inquiry should be invariably conducted in private,
Combines-Mr Manion

and that no publicity should be allowed until a finding adverse to the combine was made by the registrar.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that is all I have to say in reference to this matter, but if the Prime Minister will not think me impertinent for making another suggestion, it is this-and it has been in part covered by the remarks I have already made:	Business
is only now on the up-grade in this country, and I hope the government will not do anything which will not allow it to proceed or which will not allow it to become stable in every way. I do not like to make any remarks which would probably draw a discussion or even a criticism from some of my hon. friends opposite, but I have frequently heard it stated in this House, not out of it: "What has the government done? It has done nothing."
Hear, hear.
I am glad to hear the "hear, hear" from the other side; I expected it. Let me tell my hon. friends this
This is doing nothing twice.

Well, my right hon. friend has also endorsed what the hon. gentleman sitting behind him says. The opinion of my hon. friends, in that respect, is very much in the minority-I am waiting for them to laugh. I am urging that the government to go on the even tenor of its way is the most admirable policy that could possibly be followed at this time, because the country of all things wants stability, tranquillity; they do not want any sky-rocketing, any spectacular policies.
Will my hon. friend permit a question?
Certainly; I expected it.
Hoes he think the country wants this bill?
I have been arguing that to my hon. friend all the afternoon. I premised-
Damning it with faint praise.
I premised my remarks by saying that the spirit of the bill was admirable in every way. The bill as brought down is a basis for discussion, nothing more or less.
The hon. gentleman means that the bill is all right, only for the sections.

My right hon. friend knows perfectly well that I made no such remark.

The remarks which I made earlier in the day my right hon. friend probably regarded as not worth following, but if he had followed them closely-and I had hoped he would have; I had hoped that hon. gentlemen opposite would possibly have derived a slight amount of knowledge from my remarks od this bill-he would have heard me say definitely that the spirit of the bill was admirable but that the operation of the proposed measure and the procedure under it could bear amending, and that the bill as it stands is brought down as a basis for discussion.
When interrupted I was gomg on to say that the people were satisfied to have the government continue along the even tenor of its way and to have it avoid spectacular policies. I would therefore urge that some of the clauses of the bill be redrafted in such a manner as to carry out the spirit and intention of the bill itself.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened this afternoon and this evening with a good deal of attention to the speech of the hon. member (Mr. Marler) who has just taken his seat. I always listen to his speeches with a good deal of attention, because he studies a case before he speaks on it and he usually delivers a very thoughtful address. However, as I listened to him to-day, damning with faint praise, as somebody to my left said a few moments ago, this bill, I found myself wondering which he was endeavouring to do, to praise it or to damn it. He removed from it so far as I could see, its heart and lungs and body, and left the rest for the government, with his approval. So far as I could find, there was only one part of it with which he agreed, and that was the title.
I take very much the same attitude, Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend takes. I have listened to the other speeches; I have given some study to the bill, and I think I voice his opinion as well as my own when I say [DOT] that it is unnecessary, useless and interfering legislation. In saying this, Sir, I do not wish to be misunderstood. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in his able speech, pointed out that he did not wish to be taken as supporting trusts, combines and mergers, and I presume it is a good attitude for me to take at the beginning of the remarks that I propose to address to the House.
I may say frankly that I have not been the subject of any lobbying on this question, nor have I received even a communication of any kind in regard to it, with the exception of the ordinary circulars that I think every hon. member has received, some for and

Combines-Mr. Manion
some against the bill. I am opposing the bill in a general way, not from the legal point of view but from the general point of view that we have in this country to-day too many laws. We have laws made by this Dominion parliament, laws made by the provincial legislatures and municipal by-laws of various kinds. In fact, our statute books are cluttered up with laws of all descriptions, with most of which the people are not familiar. We are practically being legislated to death, and it is time we called a halt. Too much paternalism is being exercised, not only by this parliament, but by other legislative bodies throughout the country, and I submit that it is time to let the people do a little thinking on their own behalf. When you get on the statute books a great many laws of various kinds with which the people do not agree and of which they make, to a certain extent, a joke, you bring about a disrespect and a disregard for law which is not in the best interests of the country as a whole. I noticed some time ago in a United States paper the statement of an American senator that it was time that his country proceeded not to make more laws but to unmake many of the laws which they had already enacted. I believe' the same sentiment might well be expressed in Canada. The other day I was travelling on a train from the West, and I sat in the smoking room with a number of travellers, all strangers. An hour or two was spent by most of them-there were seven or eight-telling of the different methods by which they got around the liquor laws. It was a standing joke, and laws that are made a joke by the people are not in the best interests of any country. I repeat that such a law as that which is now proposed cannot be any more useful than other laws of past parliaments have been which had the same purpose in view, and that in adopting measures of this kind we are cluttering up our statute books with unnecessary and useless legislation.
An unfortunate feature of much legislation that is brought in is that the human element, the personal equation, is forgotten by the legislators; they have the impression that any law may be put on the statute books irrespective of how the people feel toward it. Moderation and sanity are just as necessary in lawmaking as they are in personal and public life. It is true that demagogic appeals, irrational and irresponsible in their character, are continually being made to the masses of the people, and that laws are very often enacted as the result of those appeals. But if we accede to all requests for laws of all kinds we will establish in Canada
the same type of bureaucracy which has been established in Russia and which is not doing that country any good.
I submit that this law will lead to inquisitorial investigation into private businesses, which in a great many cases would be unnecessary. It is time to leave business and industry alone, because, as has been stated by the hon. member who last spoke, we are in a time of depressed business conditions, a time which is not opportune for the bringing in of legislation which will interfere with industry generally and which can have no other effect than that of interference.
In regard to the question itself. In the first place, is this law needed? Anyone who reads section 498 of the Criminal Code will see that practically every branch of business covered by this proposed legislation is covered by that provision. It is true that some amendments might have to be made to that clause to make it more operative than it has been in the past, but at the same time I believe it has been just as operative in the past as this legislation will be in the future if it is put upon the statute books. At any rate it should not be necessary at the present time, and in the present financial condition of this country, to establish practically a new department of government with a whole staff of civil servants to look after the carrying out of such legislation as this. I believe we have in Canada to-day all the civil servants we need for the carrying on of the business of the people. I well remember the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) in a speech made in this House last year giving figures showing how year after year as the business of the country went on the cost of civil government had increased over the year previous. This legislation if it is carried out, will create a whole staff of commissioners and registrars from one end of this country to the other, and will simply be another addition to the expense of civil government without, to my mind, accomplishing the intention of the act.
In addition to that, large corporations are needed in the business world of to-day. They are needed because of the competition which is present among the different countries of the world. After all, the wheat board proposed by my friends to my left is nothing but a large combination of the same sort. It is a proposed organization for the purpose of the handling by one body of the wheat produced in the West so that we shall be able to compete in the markets of the world in that commodity. It is really a proposition along exactly the same lines as any of these organizations which are proposed to be investigated

Combines-Mr. Manion

by this legislation. The same is true of the fruit co-operative societies of British Columbia, and of some of the co-operative selling organizations of other sections of the country. Therefore, if that type of organization is necessary for the handling of the grains, for the handling of the fruit and other farm produce of this country-and I do not dispute that perhaps it is-that type of organization is all the more necessary in connection with large manufacturing plants and large industries of various kinds. Not only that, but organizations of that kind exist in all nations, and therefore have to be combatted by organizations of the same kind in countries which are in competition with them. All large organizations, even the largest trusts, do not take advantage of the opportunities the}' might take advantage of. I remember reading a short time ago The Life and Letters of Walter Hines Page, and if I remember correctly he made this statement; that during the war the time came when the necessities for oil were so great that he took it upon himself to deal with the Standard Oil Company, the greatest oil corporation in the world, on behalf of the British government and also the American government to a certain extent, and he points out that he got the finest type of co-operation from that company. Not only that, but although that trust had the opportunity of taking a large amount of money out of the coffers of the different Allies through control of the oil and gasoline that was needed by them, they did just the reverse, they cut down the price saving millions of dollars to the Allies in that regard.
We have in free trade England, and I mention this because the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans), who is not in the House at the moment so far as I can see, this afternoon blamed the whole injury to the life of this country to trusts, which he said were caused by the protective tariff-in free trade England we find trusts, mergers and combines of all kinds. I have here under my hand a report of a committee on trusts which was appointed by the British parliament in February, 1918, and reported in April, 1919. It was appointed for the purpose of looking into the advisability of bringing in just such legislation as this and in its report there is a list a page and a half long of different trusts and organizations in one line of business alone with which the Ministry of Munitions had to deal in Great Britain during the war. I will deal with that a little more fully in a moment.
Large organizations, large combines of that kind are necessary, not only because of com-

petition with other countries, as I mentioned a moment ago, but because, and it is mentioned in this report, they are able to prevent absolute bankruptcy of the smaller corporations when competition, not only internal but external, is becoming so severe that unless the smaller organizations unite and work together they will be forced into bankruptcy. Instances are given in this report of just such a condition of affairs.
Then there is the argument of the lower cost of production, cost of buying, and overhead costs. There is another important point, and in this line we have not progressed very far in Canada, and that is scientific industrial research. We have made but very little progress in this country so far as that very important branch of industry is concerned, because it is in a sense a branch of industry at the present time. It is pointed out in an appendix to this same report that it is a factor of the utmost importance that these large organizations can carry on a type of industrial research which cannot be carried on by the smaller organizations.
Then there is the question of export trade, which I mentioned a few moments ago, greater general efficiency, and finally the point made by the hon. member'for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) as to the standardization of parts. He mentioned the Ford Motor Company. Would anybody in this House contend for a moment, that if it were not for the size and strength and specialization which takes place in that organization it would be possible for it to turn out an automobile of the same quality and price as the Ford motor car at the present time? Certainly it would not be possible. So standardization of quality, standardization of parts, and specialization all add to that general efficiency and all cause a lowering in cost providing always, of course, that the organization is not permitted to take too much advantage of- possibilities which may offer because of the power of the organization. But I submit, Sir, that we have now on the statute books legislation to prevent them taking advantage of that power. I am going to quote just three or four passages from this report which I believe should be of interest to the House. The first paragraph which I quote from this report of the committee on trusts is from a statement made to them, and which the committee quote apparently approvingly, by some of the organizations with which they deal. This is the only quotation of that kind. The rest are quotations of the committee's own statements:
Where price associations exist, all members having to quote the same price, the competition among the manu-

Combines-Mr. Manion
facturers, parties to the association, becomes one of quality, and one direct and important result of these price associations is undoubtedly a tendency to rise to a general higher level in production in this respect.
Then comes a page and a half of different trusts with which the Ministry of Munitions had to deal, and regarding them the Ministry of Munitions make a statement synopsized as follows:
"VVe were furnished with detailed reports through the various departments of the ministry with regard to their experiences in dealing with these and other associations. To a very general extent these experiences appear to have been of a character satisfactory to the government. Considerable advantages were recognized in dealing with combinations and associations for war purposes. It was found that the influence of larger-minded and more moderate men had a beneficial effect upon the attitude of the trade as a whole, that the best technical advice was more easily available, and that on the whole the trade associations, and especially trade committees created for war purposes, were of the greatest assistance to the ministry.
A little further on there is another statement made by this committee,-and by the way on this committee was one of the men in England who looks upon the capitalistic system, as it is called, as a failure; I refer to Sidney Webb. I shall quote from him in a moment because he made a separate report although he signed the committee's report. This is from the full report.
It was alleged of one association that it had endeavoured to fix very exorbitant prices, and that arrangements for the control of prices had been discovered which had in fact led to a rise of prices to an excessive extent. These were, however, individual cases, and generally the officials of the ministry appeared to be of opinion that the associations had made for more economical production and for an improved quality and variety of output, and for a very beneficial interchange of technical knowledge, and that, although most associations regulated prices, the consumer in general had not suffered through such regulations.
No more favourable report upon trusts and mergers could be made, to my mind, than is contained in that statement. A little lower down there are two more statements which I wish to quote. This is one of them:
There was a general agreement among representatives of associations before us that one of the beneficial results of the formation of associations sufficiently powerful to control and maintain prices in the home market was that it enabled British manufacturers to extend then output by selling their products at a lower price, or even at a loss, in foreign markets.
I quote that because of its interest to my hon. friend for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) I am sure, and probably to others in the House, who blame the protective system for the fact that occasionally home producers sell more cheaply in the foreign market than in the home market. And yet they state here that this extensive production under free trade enables them to sell their goods more cheaply in the
foreign market than in the home market. Then they say a little lower down:
By securing remunerative prices in the home market they could make a successful bid against foreign competition in the export trade. They had a fund, a fighting fund, for the special purpose of subsidizing members who found it necessary to sell at less than an economic price in order to cut out foreign competitors. That might be called meeting dumping by dumping, but he would not agree that British firms dumped in the aggregate much more than foreign firms. They had dumped in Belgium as reprisal against Belgium dumping here.
These quotations show that the Ministry of Munitions in England, and the English government generally found large organizations, large combinations of industry, of advantage to them during the war.
Now, Sir, I have practically finished and I wish to point out in closing that in handling this matter in England this committee recommended that the whole question be handled by the Board of Trade, which is a department of the government in England just as the Department of Trade and Commerce is a department of the government in this country. They suggested bringing forward some form of legislation akin to what was in force in this country, or in New Zealand, or most of the other countries which form the British dominions, and they quoted the act of 1910 which was in force in Canada; but they leave the matter to the Board of Trade with the suggestion that a tribunal might have to be formed to handle it if the Board of Trade upon investigation found it necessary to do something to that effect; I am synopsizing the matter very briefly.
Now I wish to make one more quotation The supplementary report was made by Sidney Webb, whom I mentioned a moment ago, and three others. Mr. Sidney Webb is a gentleman who spoke of "decay of the capitalistic system" in a recent book which he wrote. While he agreed with the foregoing report and signed it-his name is attached to it-he considered that an addendum was necessary and I am going to quote one passage from it, signed by him and three others.
We do not suggest that any action should be taken to prevent or obstruct combination or association in capitalist enterprise. Apart from the experience that no such interference can be made effective,-
I should like to repeat this:
Apart from the experience that no such interference can be made effective, we have to recognize that association and combination in production and distribution are steps in the greater efficiency, the increased economy, and the better organization of industry. We regard this evolution as both inevitable and desirable. It is, however, plain that the change from competitive rivalry to combination calls for corresponding developments to secure for the community, both safeguards against the
Combines-Mr. Manion

evils of monopoly, and at least a large share of the economic benefits of the better organization of industry which it promotes.
That is praise of the whole system of large organizations. Therefore, I think it is well worth while reading because of the fact that Sidney Webb, and the other three members who agreed to the first report make the statement.
That, Mr. Speaker, is all I have to say on the question except to repeat that I consider this legislation at the present time is unnecessary and that if it is carried out, if it is put into force. I do not think it will be of any more use than the legislation which is now in force in the criminal code. I believe that industry and business in Canada is in such a shape at the present time that there should rather be a desire to leave it alone than to interfere with it unnecessarily.

Mr. Speaker, if there has been any doubt in the mind of any lion, member as to the effectiveness of the proposed legislation it is successfully answered by the quantity of literature which has been sent to the members of this House by those who have been profiting in the past and have now something to fear. I have been struck with the amount of eloquence poured out in order to whitewash these combines. I have no hesitation in saying that great combinations are necessary and that they can manufacture more efficiently and more cheaply. But that is not the trouble complained of. The point is that these combinations, or some of them, have been abusing their powers. I believe that this is an epochmaking day in the history of the present session. Now for the first time we have an opportunity, and the House is being put to the test, of passing legislation which will really have a kick in it. For many years past combinations of such a character have been growing up that at the present time we can buy no article the price of which has not been fixed arbitrarily. That is the reason we are suffering at the present time.
One hon. member opposite spoke in favour of standing pat and allowing things to remain as they are. I can assure you that I am not going to make an address of a "blue ruin" or "dry rot" character; but I have a great deal of sympathy with those who have tried to put the actual conditions of agriculture before the House. There is nothing gained by minimizing or exaggerating, when describing the conditions that prevail. To me the greatest optimist is the one who grasps and grapples with the actual problems before him and tries to solve them. There are such

problems to be solved and that is why something effective in the way of legislation ought to be enacted at this time. Combinations have been making progress in methods of getting around legislation, of devising ways and means of extracting a greater share of profit than they are entitled to, and legislation by this parliament has not kept pace with such devices. Notwithstanding all that has been said to the contrary I believe the proposed legislation to be a sincere effort to apply effective measures to prevent these combinations continuing to operate in the future as they have done in the past. Some years ago I read, in connection with American history, where an effort was made in congress to bring about more sanitary conditions in factories, to prevent child labour, and other reforms. The same arguments that we have heard to-day were then offered. When the vote took place it stood 30 for the reforms to 190 against. Four years later that vote was reversed, and the 30 had become 190. The reforms which were sought at that time were then placed on the statute book. After they were placed there everybody realized their value, and to-day nobody in the States would think of doing away with those reforms. The reform contemplated here will meet with similar opposition.
In regard to the matter of competition, we looked to competition to regulate prices in the past. When competition prevails, such legislation as this, as the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) has said is not necessary. But when competition has been strangled, as has been the case for many years in the past, something to regulate price is necessary, and I assure hon. members that if something is not done to regulate price, even those who fear this legislation, even the manufacturers, and even those who have been forming these combinations and reaping the profits, will find that the hard times will be reflected on themselves, and that they will become the sufferers. In fact they have already begun to feel the pinch and if they turn a deaf ear, and talk about standing pat when those conditions of unrest surround us, when there is need of some effective action, they will find that conditions will get worse. However, I hope I am wrong. Some people prophesy that we are now on the eve of better times. I am afraid not.
In regard to resale prices, the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) seems to uphold these organizations that have been selling at resale prices. I think the special committee on Agriculture had a little to say about that, Some witnesses gave evidence before the com-

Com bines-Mr. M illar
mittee and one witness stated that he was selling an article at SI.75 and making a very good profit, but his competitor in the same town objected because he was selling it 25 cents less than his own sale price, and the result was that the manufacturer absolutely refused to provide him with any more of those goods. That is the way the resale price works out. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre stated that they have been able to stabilize prices. They certainly have. Look at the Imperial Oil Company; they have stabilized the price of gasoline at about 55 cents a gallon in Canada when the same commodity is selling on the other side of the international boundary line at 25 cents. True there is a very slight difference in the size of their gallon.
There is no duty on gaso line. Why would a man pay 55 cents a gallon in Canada, if he could buy it on the othei side for 25 cents?
He would not make much if he had to drive 125 miles to save the 25 cents.
Does not the hon. member think the combination of the Imperial Oil Company is stronger than that of the Standard?

Perhaps when the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) is speaking, as I hope he will a little later on, he may be able to explain why gasoline is selling for 25 cents on the American side and 55 cents on the Canadian side.
I never encountered that myself.

Well I have. I have known it to be selling for 25 cents in the United States and 52 cents and 55 cents in Canada at one and the same time.
There is one section in the bill which puzzles me. It would appear to me to be difficult to find out whether a combination is guilty or not until investigation is held, and from the wording of the bill, as far as I can understand it, those combinations that are not operating against the interests of the people of Canada do not come within the jurisdiction of the registrar or inspector. I may be wrong in that, but it would seem to me there might be some difficulty there. The hon member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) has stated that we have at present too much legislation. I can understand that statement coming from those who fear legislation. Even if we have too much legislation on the statute books, that is no reason why
a bill that is really going to be effective should not be passed. I fancy that is an objection that is put forward among others in the circulars and newspaper clippings that have been circulated. I received some of them myself. It is a part of the howl of those who fear they are going to be injured by the legislation.
Referring to the statement that we have too much legislation, and that we should proceed along the even tenor of our way, let me point out that some time ago the United States went a good deal further in curbing combines and mergers than it is proposed to do by this bill, and certainly very much further than Canada has ever gone. During the time Roosevelt was President of the United States the legislation that was placed on the statute books and enforced very vigorously, was most effective and far-reaching. He took some of those large combines by the throat. He did not treat them as though those organizations were working for the welfare of the people and that they were all good. I remember reading a conversation between President Roosevelt and a representative of one of these combines who argued with him and said "Well now, you should not be hard on us; did we not provide S60.000 for your campaign fund?"
