"Yes," replied Roosevelt "but I understand you also provided $70,000 for the campaign fund of my opponent". "Well" said the former "that may be the case". During Roosevelt's regime he enforced a law such as is proposed at this time with such vigour that these organizations were curbed, and the good effect of that legislation has been felt, I believe, up to the present time.
For the sake of the hon. member's seatmate (Mr. Evans), perhaps he will admit that Roosevelt was a very strong protectionist.

The mind of the right hon. leader of the Oposition usually runs true to form, but in this particular case I think he is running off at a tangent. I do not think that has any effect whatever. Perhaps when the right hon. gentleman speaks he might explain, if the combines operating at the present time are not to the detriment of the country, why it is that gasoline is selling at 30 cents a gallon in Ottawa and selling at about 50 cents out in the West. Having been away from home some little time, I am not just prepared to say to a cent what the price of gasoline in the West is, but I think about 50 cents. Why is that so? There is a great deal the right hon. leader of the Opposition will have to explain.
Combines-Mr. Millar
Why does the hon. member ask me to explain it? I am not in office.
Everybody knows that.

I think the right hon.
leader of the Opposition among others was asking questions and seemed to disagree with me; that is the reason I asked him to make the explanation.
Not on that point.

Reference has been made to the wheat board as being something that might be classed as a combination that would come under this act. Well, I cannot conceive, from the spirit of the act as explained in the address of the Prime Minister, and from the wording of the act, that any harm would coine to the wheat board. An investigation would show that it was not intended to operate to the detriment of anybody. It was intended merely to prevent combinations from extracting from the producer a great deal of what he has a right to. But I assure the House that whether the wheat board becomes operative or not, the investigation into the lake shippers' combine and the investigation into the ocean shippers' combine will give plenty of opportunity for the operation of this bill if it is placed upon the statute books. Reports have not been issued; but the evidence has been brought out before the commission, and without the slightest doubt there is a combine that could be dealt with by this bill if it becomes law.
Let me say just a word or two in regard to unrest. It would be well at this time if hon. members would make an effort to find out the real cause of the unrest. We have been approaching this matter too much in an argumentative spirit, one trying to show that a certain industry was not getting a square deal, was getting the raw- end of the deal, and others Showing very little sympathy for it, saving: "Do not whine about it; we do not whine; why do you whine?" That is rather a dangerous course for those who are well-fed, who have been profiting from the producer and who have no reason to complain, because they have been getting the best of the deal. It is dangerous for them to take that cold-blooded, and I think I might even say, insolent attitude of "quit your whining and go to work." Much that has been said in this House might well have been left unsaid, because, as has been pointed out, this might injure the country in the matter of immigration; but unfortunate'}', it has been necessary to say what has been said, because it seemed to be impossible to enlist the sympathy of this He,use and ha.ve hon. members rea'ize the gravity of the situa-'Mr. Millar.]	'
ticn, so that they might, come to the point, where they would get together and endeavour to find a solution. That is the reason why some of our members have assumed that pessimistic attitude.
It is not all true.

An hon. member says: "it
is not all true." I assure the House that what has been said is only too true, I am sorry to say, and I regret that we have been forced into this position where we have had to speak very plainly about those adverse conditions.
In the measure that is now before the House,' an opportunity is afforded of giving effective redress; it is a measure that, if put into operation, will cause confidence to spread over the country. I am quite convinced that if those who have been suffering realize that the government mean business, that they are going to enforce this measure, and that combines that have been charging too much, that have been taking a greater share of the profits or, to put this in another way, a greater return for the services they are rendering than they should, are going to be dealt with effectively, the consuming public will be filled with confidence. This will give them, as it were, new life. Let me point to one measure that has already, I might say, given new life to the stock industry, just to show the House how effective this measure can be made. The removal of the embargo on cattle going to the Old Country, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) said a few days ago-and I agree with him-has given new life to the stock industry of the West. I assure hon. members that if this measure passes, if it is properly enforced, it will find a great deal to do; in fact, there seems to be work for it everywhere. But the moral effect will be very great. Hon. members may not believe this; some hon. members are inclined to laugh and say: "Oh, the agriculturists are always whining," but if hon. members keep on saying that, I assure them that they are taking a dangerous course. We may not always whine. We have in this country a strong foreign element, and sometimes it is necessary to keep them in curb. If the House and the country continue to take that attitude, an attitude of, as I said before, cold-blooded insolence, we may come to a time when there will be more unrest and more real trouble than we have had in the past. I would just give hon. members fair warning. Hon. members may laugh at this if they like; but that will be the effect. I am very glad to see that the

Combines-Mr. Casgrain
government has brought forward a measure that gives promise of redressing many of these evils. I know it will not be easy of enforcement; as a matter of fact, I foresee this difficulty. When the commissioner or registrar undertakes to decide whether a combination is selling for a greater price than it should, the matter of price is relative. If he takes the income of many of our people, amongst them the agriculturists, he may well decide that the combine is getting too much; but if he will take comparison with others who are drawing good salaries, he may well decide that the combine is getting enough.
I do not know how that will be decided; but, because there are difficulties in the way, I do not think is any reason why the effort should not be made. People and parliaments stand at their best, they are in their greatest glory when they are accomplishing that which seems almost impossible. This seems a difficult task; but I do not think it is impossible, and I certainly will give it my hearty support.
Mr. PIERRE F. CASGRAIN (Charlevoix-Montmorency):	Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend
(Mr. Millar) in connection with this bill, used the impression, "if it was an effective measure." We seem to have had before a few effective measures like the one that has been presented to the House. In 1919, under the Union government, there were introduced the bill for the establishment of the famous Board of Commerce and the Combines and Fair Prices bill to prevent abuses and to reduce the cost of living. We know what thr result of that legislation was. The act was in existence for just a few months when one after another of the gentlemen who were on the board resigned, contending that, under the bill as it was drafted and even with the powers that were given to them, they were not able to enforce the legislation. Under the old Laurier regime, there was introduced the act of 1907, and the bill which is at present before the House seems to be very much like a repetition of- that act which fell into disuse and apparently was enforced against only one big organization of the United States which was doing business in this country, with the result at that time that there was a slight modification introduced into their way of doing business. Apparentlv, however, there were in this country other combines or other similar institutions; but the act was not directed at them, and the people did not resort to the means put into their hands to have an investigation into those organizations. The motive underlying the bill is undoubtedly a good one. The Prime Minister and the government want to do what is
fair and right by the people, and undoubtedly this measure is introduced in redemption of the pledge contained in the Speech from the Throne, to wit:
A bill will be submitted to you to safeguard the interests of consumers and producers from undue enhancement of prices or unfair restriction of trade by combines, monopolies, trusts or mergers.
I would draw the particular attention of the House to the phrase, "undue enhancement of prices." But although this bill is drafted with the intention of safeguarding the interests of consumers and producers from undue enhancement of prices or unfair restriction of trade, I am afraid that it will fail of its purpose unless it is amended in several particulars. Far be it from me to criticize the bill in a spirit out of sympathy with the policy of the government. I endorse the action taken by the government and congratulate the Prime Minister on the introduction of this bill, which is but another evidence of his desire to better the condition of the working classes and those engaged in a small way of business and to protect them against the big interests. However, it is apparent from the constructive criticism which we have heard from the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) that the bill if allowed to remain in its present form will not accomplish what is intended.
I find several objections to the bill as drafted. In the first place, I am afraid that the provision against the fixing of a common or a resale price by merchants, traders, or manufacturers would unduly hamper our domestic trade without curing the abuses which the bill is directed against. To carry out this provision would mean intermeddling and interference with the conduct of business and would bring about exactly the opposite result to that which the government has in view. I believe our industries should be given every encouragement and should not be dealt with unjustly -in fact they should be treated just as fairly as the public whom we wish to protect.
Another defect in the bill is that any person of the age of 21 is empowered to lay a complaint, but nothing is said as to whether he must be a British subject. No doubt this is an oversight on the part of the draftsmen, and will be corrected when the bill is in committee.
The definition of the word "combine" in the second section in my opinion is objectionable. The definition is neither precise nor scientific in its terms and it is impossible to ascertain from it what really is a combine within the meaning of the section. This definition should be recast in order that we may have no trouble when the bill becomes law.
Combines-Mr. Casgrain

It will be remembered that in the case of the Board of Commerce the law was tested in the Supreme Court and found to be unconstitutional. I am afraid we may have similar trouble here unless we go through this bill very carefully and all our time and trouble will have been wasted.
Another defect to my mind is that the bill does not appear to contain any provision that the person laying a complaint shall give a guarantee of his good faith. All he has to do is to simply write a letter to the registrar and the machinery of the law is set in motion. In all proceedings in our criminal courts when a complaint is laid regarding a matter of minor importance the complainant must appear before the magistrate and give his reasons for believing that he is entitled to the redress that he is seeking, and, moreover, he must deposit five dollars. Under this bill any person who may have a grudge against his employer can either personally or by letter set the law in motion. I think there should be an amendment requiring the complainant to make a sworn statement before the registrar, rendering the procedure similar to that required in ordinary criminal matters. Furthermore, I think where the word "opinion" occurs in this bill it is objectionable. As I said before, there ought to be some reasons given by the complainant as in ordinary criminal proceedings. When a person lays a complaint in our criminal courts we always take the trouble of asking him if he has good reason to believe that his complaint is justified. In this particular instance I think the bill should be amended accordingly in order to protect the public at large, and I do not think it would be going too far to require a security from the person who invokes the law, such security to depend on the nature and gravity of the complaint that is laid. As was suggested by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, I think it would be well to follow the wording in the old law, which provided, if I recollect correctly, that only upon at least five persons alleging a series of breaches of the law could the machinery be set in motion. One single case of too high a price should not be ground to justify an investigation. Where there is a series of repeated infractions of the law they become injurious to the whole community, and thereupon the law should be put into force.
Sections 5, 6 and 9 do not appear to me to be very plain; indeed, reading them in conjunction with section 10 I see no reason why a third investigation may not be ordered.
I Mr. Casgrain.]
I think it should be made very clear that a preliminary investigation before a registrar or commissioner must be made of every complaint, unless this discloses reasonable and proper grounds for believing that the complaint is well founded, no further steps should be taken; if reasonable and proper grounds are disclosed, then a commissioner should be appointed to thoroughly investigate the complaint. But as the bill now stands there appears to be nothing to prevent the registrar or commissioner from holding two or three investigations on the very same matter.
The question of secrecy has been touched upon by the .hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I do not think the bill is sufficiently clear on this point. It is all very well to investigate the affairs of any industrial or business concern. * But I do not believe that the law sufficiently protects these people; I am not sure that persons or firms appearing before the commissioner would not suffer considerably through the exposure to the public of their business affairs, their business methods, and so on.
I notice also that although this law follows in certain respects our criminal procedure it does not give to the accused or to the person who appears before the registrar or commissioner the rights given to one who appears before our courts. I do not see anything in the bill which gives to the person brought before the commissioner or registrar the light to be represented by counsel. It would, in my opinion, be a denial of justice to have the law passed in that form; I submit that there should be provision under which any person who is charged with having violated the law should have the right from tha outset to bring in his own lawyer and have his interests properly protected. There is also a clause in the bill which states that evidence may be brought in in the form of affidavits. That is altogether against the practice in the province of Quebec-I do not know how it is in the other provinces-because one who is a party to an action in our province has always the right to hear the witnesses on either side, to cross-examine them and test their veracity. As the bill is drafted, anyone charged with violating the provisions of this law would not have that right if an affidavit only was produced.
I do not see in the law any provision for appeal. I regard it as very necessary that the accused or the person brought before the commissioner should have the right of appeal if the decision is adverse to him. In section 498 of the Criminal Code, which at present protects the public in regard to these

Combines-Mr. Woodsworth
matters, there is provision for appeal, and I think that in this law we ought to have a similar provision to what is contained in Article 1012 of the Criminal Code of Quebec, which enables appeal to be oaken from conviction.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, 1 may say that I have not so much objection to the bill as it is drawn as I have to what is not contained in the bill. The principle of the proposed law is a good one, but it would seem as if it had been conceived and put before us with, perhaps, too great haste, and if we discuss it a little longer we shall probably be able to bring out its defects and devise the necessary amendments for its improvement. The first thing that ought to be done is, in my opinion, to remodel the definition and to provide that only persons who are British subjects shall have the right to avail themselves of the provisions of the proposed law. It should be provided also that the complainant shall state under oath that he has just leason for believing that the law has been violated. There should also be a provision to ensure that the evidence adduced shall not be made public and thus injure or prejudice ihe interests of the person who is charged with violation. And, as I said a moment ago, the l.ght of appeal should be provided, thus conforming to the provision contained in Article 1012 of the Criminal Code of the province of Quebec.
Lastly, I find no mention made in the bill as to who the commissioner is going to be - whether it is to be an official of some department, or otherwise. The law does not state whether or not the commissioner shall be a lawyer. I do not want to speak on behalf of my own profession, but i>
is the experience that when a person other than a lawyer is appointed to such a position the law has not always been carried out as it should be. I believe that the registrar or the commissioner ought to be a competent lawjer of at least ten years' standing and experience at the provincial bar, in order that justice may be done to all and that the interests of none may be prejudiced.

Mr. Speaker, in introducing this bill the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that it would be specially interesting to those who were engaged in the process of production, and to the consumers. Yet I fancy that a great many of the labour people, who constitute the great bulk of producers of the country and who are decidedly consumers, will not consider that in this bill we have anything that really is vital or that will adequately meet present needs. I was delighted
a little while ago to hear the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) quoting Sidney Webb in favour of combinations. Undoubtedly we must recognize that the greater number of the labour people and the socialists, both in this country and Great Britain, are in favour of combinations. They do not fail to realize the evils existing in connection with combinations as they are at present, but they do recognize the inevitability of combines. In tracing the development of our present industrial system, we believe that this is one step forward and that we are now in a position where we shall have to take, in the near future, another step forward. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River did not elaborate the position taken by Mr. Webb and the other Fabian socialists. He did not quote from Mr. Webb's latest book, "The Decay of Capitalist Civilization," in which Mr. Webb points out that we have been travelling for a considerable time along the line of the concentration of capital in the hands of a comparatively small group; that this system is failing to fulfil the primary function of meeting the needs of the people, and hence is on its trial. Mr. Webb is far from taking the attitude of the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River that we should let well enough alone; with other Fabian socialists, and I think with the workers generally, he says it is inevitable that we should take another step and that in the immediate future.	,
We recognize that the combinations we have in industry and commerce to-day, as well as in finance-the latter a later development-are largely the outgrowth of the industrial revolution that took place in Great Britain one hundred and fifty years ago. When the factory system came into existence and the individual workman gave up his little home workshop and went into the factory, we entered upon a new period in the development of industry, the period of combinations-and we cannot avoid the consequences. In those early days of the new age when the machine threatened to take the very bread out of the mouths of their children the workers in desperation threatened to break the machine. They thought that this was the only way of attaining their end. They learned in later days that what they should have done was to have gained possession of the machine. Now there are those who fearful of the combinations, of the elaborate organization which has been set up on the basis of the physical machine, would try to break up the combinations, break up the elaborate organization. We take the ground that such a policy would be as fatal as the machine-smashing policy of

Combines-Mr. Woodsworth
one hundred and fifty years ago. It is impossible for us effectively to break up these combines. The only possible thing for us to do if we want really effective action is to take hold of them and carry them one step further until we have such a complete combine that the public through its various organizations co-operative, municipal, provincial and federal, will be able to use it for its own purposes.
The Prime Minister said that in this age of competition combinations are necessary. I submit that if this can be called the age of competition it must be pointed out that it is competition of different groups and that constantly these competing groups tend to combine into larger units, so that after all the earlier age of individual competition has passed by. This is essentially the age of combination, and in so far as we still have competition it is indicative of incomplete development. It may be true that to-day we need combinations of the different warring groups; it is only because we are in the process of development, and We must inevitably face the formation of larger and yet larger combinations.
The Prime Minister says that he does not seek to prevent just combinations, but what does he mean by just combinations? Who is to decide what is just? I am not using the term just; that is the Prime Minister's term; I am not using the term unjust. The fact is that we have to deal with an existing institution, a combination, and we do not get very far by saying that it is just or that it is unjust. It is in its very nature a form of industrial organization which gives power to a limited group, and as the process goes on, the power becomes so great that the public welfare is threatened.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said that he was desirous of eliminating useless competition. Again the whole question is raised as to what is useless competition or when competition may be useful. Are we not here again face to face with the fact that competition represents a transitory stage, and that we look forward more and more to combination, co-operation taking the place of competition. I take it that our stand on this question must be that competition is inevitable, and the Prime Minister and the government, however sincere in introducing a bill of this character, are attempting to do what is in reality impossible. I do not think there is any state in any part of the world that has attempted to curb the natural development of combinations that has found it was able to do so effectively. Probably the hon. member for Vancouver Centre showed sufficiently how difficult it is to administer legis-
lation of this character. Inevitably as you try to curb combination you come into contact with others who are perhaps less advanced in their combination, and so conflict is sure to result. Our position is that combination is not only inevitable, but that the thoroughgoing regulation of it is futile. I should like to quote what is probably as good a statement of a popular criticism of the principle of the bill as could be found. The writer of this editorial, which was circulated throughout the West, is trying to show that arbitrary power would be given into the hands of the government through the registrar. He says:
If the registrar is to have power to decide what is an unfair price it follows that he must have the authority to say what is fair price. This is the logical working out of the proposed act. Are the men and women who produce or sell potatoes, milk, bread, magazines and the thousand commodities that are in daily use prepared to have a government official set their prices for them?
Is there a man to whom the public would be willing to hand over this power? Is it fair to any man to ask him to make decisions of this nature? What kind of a job would the registrar have? Are there such supermen in the country? If there are, might they not be employed in other and more consequential departments of the government service?
That sounds reasonable, but when we come to consider the situation as it is about us at the present time we shall have to confess that very small groups and, in some cases, single individuals do as a matter of fact decide what these prices shall be. I have known a good many towns where the price of milk is decided by one company. I have known a great many towns throughout the West where the price of meat is decided by one corporation. I think that nearly all of us can point to article after article where the price is decided by one individual, and the trouble is that to-day that individual is responsible to no one but himself or his company. He is not in any sense responsible to the public at large. If we are to have combinations, let us have combinations that we can control. Let us have combinations and let us appoint officials to administer them who will decide their policies with a view to the public interest.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) was very much afraid of having six people placed in a position where they could bring any charge or set in motion the machinery for having an investigation. Now it does seem to me that we need not worry about that. I take it that in other matters one individual can bring against another man a charge of the most serious nature. He can say that a man is suspected of being guilty of murder. If he has information that leads him to believe that, it

Combines-Mr. Woodsworth
becomes his duty to give that information to the state. I do not know that most of us are in danger of being accused of murder because that course is open to any citizen. The fact is that if there are no abuses these charges are not likely to be laid. I do not object to the suggestion that was thrown out recently that we have these matters brought seriously before the public by way of an affidavit or something of that kind. But in any case the humblest individual in the state ought to be able to invoke the protection of the state against any of these big interests. I think I am voicing the opinion of a great many people when I say that to-day we are more afraid of the big combinations with all the prestige which they possess and all the money that is behind them than we are of the irresponsibility of a few individuals who perhaps for some private grudge might bring forward some charge that was baseless. After all, if the charge is baseless, provision is made in the bill whereby it can be investigated in a preliminary way by the registrar, before it goes on to a more thorough investigation. If the charge is baseless why should any firm or corporation fear the fullest and freest investigation? The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) would like also I believe, to take away the safeguards to labour which are contained in section 34. This section reads as follows:
Nothing in this act shall be construed to apply to combinations of workmen or employees for their own reasonable protection as such workmen or employees.
That section is much along the line of existing legislation and simply seeks to protect the workmen from action which unfortunately has been taken sometimes in the past to prevent them from organizing. In the old days professional workers had a right to combine. No one ever questioned that right, and we have combinations of lawyers, doctors, newspaper men, authors, and so on. But when the workers some one hundred years ago, began to combine it was a different story. It was said they had no right to combine, no right whatever, and so later on certain special legislation had to be introduced to safeguard their interests. I should like to ask why the workers should not be allowed the fullest right to organize? That right is in fact guaranteed under the Peace treaty of Versailles. Why should they not have that right as much as business and professional men? We have the Canadian Manufacturers' Association-a great combination which is exercising a tremendous influence and very largely, I maintain, influencing the fiscal policy of this country. We
have railway associations which, according to the reports of the recent commission, appeal to have exercised their combination in such a way that there has been a very real restraint of trade. We have shipping combinations at the present time. We have a banking association which is distinctly a close corporation We had even mentioned here on the floor of the House a newspaper combination. I cannot see why there should be any objection whatever to allow the fullest right to labour employees, of any class whatever, to combine and, in my opinion, if it is necessary to do so their interests ought to be effectively safeguarded.
There are one or two points in the bill which I should like to criticize, points which some have criticized from the opposite angle. The Prime Minister says that information, in connection with proceedings under the bill, will not be made public. I should like to ask why not? Why should there be any secrecy connected with these investigations? It seems to me that in such a provision we are, perhaps, going back to the ideals of an earlier state of industry when industry was essentially private and almost personal in its character. None of us want men to come into our homes and pry into our private affairs; but a great modern business is by no means a private enterprise. When there are a large number of people associated with it, it thereby becomes public, and the public have definite rights in regard to what is going on in connection with it. The Prime Minister said that publicity would do more than penalties to remove evils. I believe that is true. Why then should we not have the very fullest publicity in connection with this matter? In connection with this feature I was reminded of a treatment of this question which was given nearly ten years ago by ex-President Woodrow Wilson. May I be permitted to quote several paragraphs from his work "The New Freedom" which seem very pertinent to the point under discussion.
We used to say that the ideal of government was for every man to be left alone and not interfered with, except when he interfered with somebody else; and that the best government was the government that did as little governing as possible. That was the idea that obtained in Jefferson's time. But we are coming now to realize that life is so complicated that we are not dealing with the old conditions, and that the law has to step in and create new conditions under which we may live, the conditions which will make it tolerable for us to live.
Let me illustrate what I mean: It used to be true in our cities that every family occupied a separate house of its own, that every family had its own little premises, that every family was separated in its life from every other family. That is no longer the case in our great cities. Families live in tenements, they live in flats, they live on floors; they are piled layer upon
2554.

Combines-Mr. Woodsworth
layer in the great tenement houses of our crowded districts, and not only are they piled layer upon layer, but they are associated room by room, so that there is in every room, sometimes, in our congested districts, a separate family. In some foreign countries they have made much more progress than we in handling these things. In the city of Glasgow, for example (Glasgow is one of the model cities of the world), they have made up their minds that the entries and the hallways of great tenements are public streets. Therefore, the policeman goes up the stairway, and patrols the corridors; the lighting department of the city sees to it that the halls are abundantly lighted. The city does not deceive itself into supposing that that great building is a unit from which the police are to keep out and the civic authority to be excluded, but it says: "These are public highways, and light is needed in them, and control by the authority of the city."
I liken that to our great modern industrial enterprises. A corporation is very like a large tenement house; it isn't the premises of a single commercial family; it is just as much a public affair as a tenement house is a network of public highways.
When you offer the securities of a great corporation to anybody who wishes to purchase them, you must open that corporation to the inspection of everybody who wants to purchase. There must, to follow out the figure of the tenement house, be lights along the corridors, there must be police patrolling the openings, there must be inspection wherever it is known that men may be deceived with regard to the contents of the premises. If we believe that- fraud lies in wait for us4 we must have the means of determining whether our suspicions are well founded or not.
I do not think there is anywhere a better statement of the character of modern industry and the necessity of having these big corporations wide open to public inspection. I do not see why we should talk any longer about business secrets; developments have carried us beyond that stage. The member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in criticizing the bill said that combination ought to be considered a crime only when there is a combination to deliberately injure competitors. It strikes me, although I am not a lawyer, that that is rather a novel position. It would seem that in many departments of law injury does not have to be deliberate in order that it should be made a crime. Why, we have even such a phrase as "criminal neglect" to condemn people who under certain circumstances do not do anything at all; but it is recognized that they should do something. Now, if we have a combination that has the effect of injuring the community surely that is a good reason why that particular combination should be made a criminal one. I do not know a better statement of the case than was given by the Prime Minister himself when he said that private rights cease when they involve public wrongs. So then in each case we come back to the question as to whether any particular form or association is in the interests of the public or is contrary to their interests. We find that through the course of years,
IMr. Woodsworth.]
with no particular guilt on the part of any one, we have arrived at these great industrial, commercial, financial institutions which we call combines, mergers and trusts. I take it that we are not here to-night blaming the individuals who, perhaps, have had a larger share of initiative and have organized these big combinations. We are not saying that the combines should not have been organized. They probably represent a distinct step in advance of the old unorganized' stage of society, the old free competition that used to exist fifty or a hundred years ago, but on the other hand no one .can consider their social effects without realizing that they have placed in the hands of a very small group of individuals an immense power, not only in this country, but in all countries. There is to-day a life and death struggle as to whether the industrial, commercial and financial organizations that have grown up in the last hundred years will be supreme and control even our political organizations, or whether the political organizations which grew up under an earlier system of production, are going to adapt themselves with sufficient rapidity, and are capable of asserting their control over the newer industrial organizations which now rival them in power. I take it that to-night we are helping to decide that struggle. If this House is true to the people that it represents, it will definitely set itself to attack our great problems. I welcome this bill because it gives a certain measure of publicity, because it calls public attention to the evils which exist and to the necessity for further action. I cannot become tremendously enthusiastic about it, because it is negative in its character, it simply seeks to stem the inevitable incoming tide of greater combinations. I could hope that in some way we could recognize the good that lies in combinations, in the formation of larger industrial and social units, and that as a House we could begin in a democratic way, to operate these larger units.

The constituency I represent, containing as it does somewhere in the neighbourhood of a hundred thousand people, has within its borders special manufacturers who, through the course of building up their business have fixed prices and claim that, in order to carry on their business in the way they have built it up, they must continue to fix prices. This bill, as I read it, does not say that the manufacturers must not fix a retail price, but it does say, in the words of the Prime Minister, that when they do fix that retail price, it must not be to the detriment of the general public. Now what is the present law on the

Combines-Mr. Healy
subject? In reference to the Board of Commerce Act of 1919 and the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1922 the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council held thac both 'these acts were ultra vires. In reference to the bill before the House to-night, I hope the Prime Minister will ask the Deputy Minister of Justice to be sure that the proposed bill is not ultra vires of this parliament. It would be in my opinion a very grave injustice to the people of this country if after this bill was passed, and after many attempts to enforce it, the discovery should finally be made that this parliament had no right to pass such an act.
I agree absolutely with the general principles of this bill, but I do not agree altogether with the way that it may be enforced. In the district I represent we have large manufacturers who have built up their plants. I refer, for instance, to the Ford Company which has been mentioned by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). I wish to thank them for advertising the constituency from which I come. Both of these hon. members paid a visit to that constituency during the last campaign. I am glad to say we will welcome them at any time. I hope that they will come and definitely settle in my constituency, but of course, I will not guarantee that they can come back here, representing that constituency. I wish to thank them for advertising the great Ford Company of Canada. This company, after twenty years' experience in business building up, that wonderful organization, and building up on a fixed policy of a resale price from the dealer to the public, have produced a manufacturing concern that today, using the highest-priced labour in the world, is turning out the lowest priced motor car in the British dominions, and they are further attempting to increase their production to such an extent that these two factors shall be brought closer together, and surely, Mr. Speaker, that is something worth working for, when the money made can be turned to the benefit both of the consumer and of the man who produces the article and supplies the labour.
So I think that concerns such as this,-and I have taken it as an example-are rather worried over the proposed legislation, which contemplates the appointment of so many registrars. The bill does not say that these registrars shall be experienced in law. As this bill stands at present, a registrar may be any amateur who is appointed by the minister. If we were to have the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the present Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) in power forever, I do not think this country would have much to fear from this provision. If the registrars are to do any work under this bill, if this bill is to be of any benefit to the country, they will have a large quantity of work to do, and we shall have to have registrars in all sections of Canada. There may be one in the Yukon, there may be one in Prince Edward Island; there may be one in British Columbia, and any six individuals in any one of these provinces, or, for that matter, in any city, can ask that, for instance, the company about which I am talking shall be investigated. I see in this bill nothing to prevent six individuals in each of a number of towns throughout the country, asking for an investigation of the same company at the same time. From the way in wihch this measure is drawn, I cannot see that a registrar would be justified in preventing such an investigation from going on in different parts of the country at the same time and of the same corporation. I can see that such registrars might arrive at different conclusions, and I can see that when the question came before the minister for final decision, he might be in a very serious frame of mind how he should decide. Therefore, if at a*U possible, these registrars and also the commissioners should be men trained in the law. I believe the people of this country and, in particular, of the province of Ontario are sick and tired of having regulatory laws put into force by amateurs. We in our constituency suffered terribly from amateurs attempting to put into force a certain law. The thing was a nightmare. This country is, perhaps, tired of anything that smacks of uplift legislation, anything that has a tendency to appear as muck-raking legislation.
The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) mentioned this afternoon a certain combination in this country, and I hope when this bill is put into force, one of the first combinations to be investigated will be the newspaper combination. I say that not with the idea at all of criticising newspaper men. I noticed that a partcular combination was spoken of, and I know it is a combination of about twenty-nine men who absolutely control the telegraphic news of this country. This combination was known as the Canadian Press, but I believe the name was changed. Not all the members of this newspaper association agree with its practice, because in a case that I was interested in a member of the association from Quebec, Mr. Gagnon-I have not the pleasure of knowing this gentleman [DOT]-'another member from Toronto, Mr. Irving
Combines-Mr. Healy

Robertson, and another member from London, Mr. Ford, stood out and said that they did not believe this association should take the stand they had taken in certain cases. This association, as I say, is a combination of about twenty-nine of the daily newspapers; the weekly newspapers are not in the combination, and they do not get the telegraphic news. This combination is and has been subsidized from year to year by the people of Canada to the extent of $50,000 per year, and this has been done under several governments. I am not quite satisfied that if we are going to pass legislation in restraint of combinations, the people of Canada should continue to subsidize any organisation which absolutely takes it upon itself to keep a newspaper out of any particular city or town. I take this occasion to bring to the attention of the House this combination, because I think it is an outstanding combination in this country that needs investigation. I am quite aware, of course, when I make these remarks about this association, that there is no doubt at all of what they will think of me; but when a man is appointed by the people to represent them in parliament, when he sees something that he thinks should be remedied, he should have no hesitation whatever in getting upon his feet and saying what he thinks about the matter.
I agree with the general principles of this bill. I believe manufacturers and business men are just as honest as any other class of citizdns in this country. I suppose there are amongst manufacturers and business men the same proportion of crooks-perhaps no more and no less-as there are amongst professional men, newspaper men and farmers. Therefore, I believe it is necessary to have legislation to catch crooks wherever they are, and to punish crooks when they are caught.
If in the opinion of this government, it is necessary to have legislation in this form, I am willing to subscribe to it and to vote in favour of it. But I hope the Prime Minister may see his way clear, so that business concerns such as the one I have described, comprising those who are trying to specialize on certain articles, to increase production and to lower prices to the consumers, may, if possible, be left out of the investigations that may be necessary under this legislation. Unless investigation is absolutely necessary for the general welfare of this country, these concerns should not be bothered by any such inquiries as are provided for in this measure.
As regards the penalty clause, a corporation is only fined, and there is no opportunity of imprisoning the master mind of such an organization. If they are powerful and wealthy enough, a fine of $25,000 is

not sufficient punishment, and in each of these organizations some officer should be made responsible who will take the gaol sentence, in case they are found guilty, just the same as any other porch-climber or burglar would go to gaol in case of an ordinary theft. This bill does not provide for any such punishment; it provides simply for a fine in the case of a corporation, and we all know how simple it is for a person to change into a corporation. That change can be effected under both provincial and federal law in a very simple manner, and then of course there is no one left to take the gaol sentence, and a little fine will settle all the trouble. I say "a little fine," because it is considered little to the interests concerned.
The point I want to make is this: If the law is necessary it should be made drastic enough to really punish the guilty; if it is not necessary it should not be placed Upon the statute books. I agree that some such law is necessary, but I do not think it should be just in the form of this bill. I believe that the form of the bill can be changed in such a manner that legitimate business will not be worried, while combinations detrimental to the public interest will be punished. Another danger that may arise under this bill, as I said before, is the multiplication of officials. If it were possible to confine the administration of this proposed law to our courts, many of the objections as I see them would disappear.
In conclusion of these brief remarks, Sir, I wish to say that I do not think it is wrong for a man to attempt to criticize the form of proposed legislation the principle of which he is willing to support. When I entered public life one of the determining factors for my action was my absolute confidence in the Prime Minister and his cabinet and since I have been a member of this House I have seen and heard nothing to lead me to abate my confidence in the slightest degree. I still have the most absolute confidence that the Prime Minister is trying to do the very best he can for the people of this country, I also fully believe that the members of his cabinet are actuated by the same motives, and while I object to the form of this measure, if after due consideration by the Prime Minister and his cabinet they cannot see their way clear to amend its form, then, although I shall regret their inability to do so, I shall still subscribe to the general principle embodied in the bill and give it my support.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I desire to offer

Combines-Mr. Meighen
a few remarks on this measure. I do not intend to administer anything in the way of criticism of its provisions one by one. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, if I find myself unable to agree with the printed bill I will not be able to glorify its authors with the same meek humility and partisan credulity of some hon. members. I was indeed amused at the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). He reviewed the measure, took one feature and then another, showed to his own satisfaction that they were wholly wrong, told us that the bill aimed at repressing evil and unjust combinations, but that its actual provisions had the effect instead, of repressing good combinations; but notwithstanding all that was wrong about the bill, he was quite certain that it proceeded out of a pure and holy source.
When the resolution was before the House I reviewed very briefly the history of our anti-combine legislation so called. I am going to ask the House to bear with me while I do so again, because although we may take this section and that section and say it does not read as if it would be effective, or that it does, yet we cannot, get a comprehensive view of the real question we are discussing except in the light of the history of this legislation from the earliest times.
Hon. gentlemen talk of agreeing with the principle of this bill, and then end their speeches without the slightest indication of what they conceive the principle of the bill to be. I was indeed anxious to learn from the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Healy) what is this principle as to which he expresses such profound approval, in the presence of which he is going to vote for the bill, no matter what its form-in other words-what its provisions may be. What is this sacred, sanctimonious principle?
A square deal to everyone in this country.
Well, if such is the principle of the bill how is it that it does not do this for the hon. gentleman's constituents, the Ford Company?
I believe it does in principle and in final result, but it is the form of putting it in operation that I criticize.

What is the difference
about the form if the result is all right? Where does this kind of talk get us? I think it was Mr. Balfour who stated that the most foul smelling of platitudes was this continual talk about "a square deal and justice" with [DOT] no reference to specific enactments.
This bill, to my mind, instead of being a measure seeking to get concrete results is a measure distinctly seeking to avoid them. I believe a recital of our legislation will show that wherever in the past we have had provisions that really stretched forth and caught somebody they are left out of this bill, but everything is here which is going to pile harassments, vexation and expense on legitimate business; that is all in the measure- investigation after investigation, circle after circle, but never any goal.
In 1888 parliament sought first to enact anti-combine legislation and a committee sat to work out some effective measure. It was passed in 1889, with amendments in 1892 and, I am inclined to think, a further amendment later, all of them as to the wording varying the original act in very slight form. The act of 1889 constitutes what is now clause 498 of our Criminal Code. In 1910 parliament enacted the Combines Investigations Act supplementary to that provision of the Criminal Code,, which provision has been in our law ever since it was enacted in 1889.
The Combines Investigations Act had for its object the investigating of such institutions as six persons alleged to constitute a combine. "Combine" was defined, but not in the terms of this bill. The definition of the word in this bill I will deal with later. It is taken almost verbatim from the definition in a subsequent act. The Combines Investigations Act, however, proved to be aimless legislation, it proved to reach out to no real result.
Hon. gentlemen have spoken-the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), I remember particularly-about the law's delay, the procrastination of our courts, and he pleaded for a measure like this that gets at investigation in a simple way and, according to his idea, more expeditiously. Well, under the Combines Investigation Act, ,the provisions for investigation imder which were much the same as this, there was only one investigation. Instead of being expeditious the investigation lived out the whole length of the dying days of one government and well through the young virility of the next and ended in nothing but mist. I refer to the investigation into the United Shoe Machinery Company. It provided for investigation, provided for the summoning of witnesses-all sorts of inquisition-and finally provided for a verdict. Then, if there was to be any punishment, if there was to be any injunction, if there was to be any variation of practice on the part of the "combinester," the whole process had to be gone over again
Combines-Mr. Meighen

before the criminal courts. I have briefly defined the Combines Investigation Act. This act is not in every respect the Combines Investigation Act. I have at least given the whole result of that act; there was no other prosecution under it.
Before I proceed to the next piece of legislation let me remark this:	There
have been numerous prosecutions under our Criminal Code. Under what is now section 498 there have been numerous prosecutions in our criminal courts, successful prosecutions too; and what is more, there have been civil proceedings which have been determined upon the provisions of that section of the Criminal Code. I believe that section has been a comparatively effective and useful section, though I do not contend for a moment that it could not now be amended with advantage. I will refer to this sentence again later.
Now I have dealt with the initial legislation-section 498 as it is to-day; then the Combines Investigation Act in 1910. The next legislation was in the form of two bills passed in 1919, assented to on the 7th of July of that year, one of them the Combines and Fair Prices Act and the other the Board of Commerce Act. The Combines and Fair Prices Act defined a combine I think in every particular the same as it is defined here; if there is any change it is a very trifling change. The Combines and Fair Prices Act then proceeded on the assumption that combines were not nece-mrily against the public interest, were not necessarily wrong, might even be beneficial; and it proceeded to define the powers of a board in the way of curtailing the activities of wrong combines, altering their methods, preventing malpractice, and so forth. It proceeded to establish it as a crime for any company or any person to d i vhat it was, after investigation, forbidden to do !y that beard. It stated as well that the being privy or party to a combine as defined by the act, was in itself a crime. The Board of Commerce Act covered another sphere, namely, the fixing of profits. What I want to emphasize as the outstanding provision of the Combines and Fair Prices Act is that it established a board with power to prevent and power to compel. It vested in that board the right to prevent any company or combination of companies, which had been established before it as carrying on practice detrimental to the public interest, from continuing those practices. Within that board rested the power to order them to do this, the power to order them not to do that. I do not think legislation in any

country ever went further. Whether it went too far or not there is a difference of opinion. Those times, however, were different from these: then profits were being made; then business was ex-tremel3r active-we are living in different times to-day. I am emphasizing this: that the Board of Commerce under the Combines and Fair Prices Act had effective and final power to deny certain practices existing or to compel certain things to be done necessary to compliance with the law and make the combination no longer against the interests of the public. Of course the Board of Commerce as well had power to exhibit its findings, its evidence, its returns, and its documents before the attorney general of any province, thereby inviting the attorney general, if he thought fit, to conduct prosecution within that province before the criminal courts.
We now come to this legislation. This legislation establishes a board, but the name is changed; there has been a rechristening. A man is to be appointed called a registrar, and then around him at different times and different places there may be appointed commissioners. For all practical purposes I think it is fair to say that the registrar corresponds with the chairman of the old Board of Commerce and that the commissioners correspond with the puisne commissioners of the Board of Commerce. They have certain powers; and what are those powers? Now, I want to address myself to those who, without, I think, very thorough inquiry into the measure, have assumed that there are some teeth in its provisions. What are the powers of these men?	They have power to
investigate, yes; they can investigate, in private, or in	public if ordered by
the minister.	They can lay the result
before the minister, and if the minister is not satisfied he can order them to make further inquiry, and presumably they go on and inquire again. If he is not satisfied with the next report he can order another inquiry and they can proceed around the circle once more. But after they have done all their inquiry, in public or in private; after all are completed, they cannot order anybody to do anything or to stop doing anything; they have no executive power. Those attributes which the Board of Commerce possessed, the functionaries erected by this legislation are stripped of altogether. Well, what can they do? They report to the minister and the minister can lay the facts before the attorney general of the province. The old Board of Commerce could dc that, but the old Board of

Combines-Mr. Meighen
Commerce could as well say what in the future should be right as respects a certain practice, what should be done and what should not be done. The functionaries erected here have no such power at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I ask my right hon. friend, when be is speaking of the Board of Commerce, if he would tell the House what particular functions of the board were declared to be ultra vires of the federal parliament?

I am coming to that- and I will guarantee to come to it, too; I will not avoid it. They can expose the facts before the Attorney General as the old board could. There is this in addition-from memory I do not think it was in the Board of Commerce Act-that if the Attorney General of any province declines within three months to act, the Solicitor General himself may lay an indictment, on the relation, it says, of anybody over twenty-one years of age. I pause only to remark that the addition of that clause is pure surplusage, if indeed, I should not describe it as pure sham, for the reason that without any clause at all the federal Attorney General can lay an indictment, the Solicitor General can lay an indictment, can enter a prosecution.	He does not need any clause
of a new act to do that. May I remark once more before going further that all this power of inquiry that is supposed to be such a tremendous step in advance leads nowhere, that after it is through it does not end in anything, your registrar having no power to order anything done or to stop anything being done. But the whole of it could be done without any new statute whatever. It could be done under our Inquiries Act to-day. I repeat, there is not a single thing that may be done under this legislation that the government is not already competent to do under legislation that this House passed years ago.
Nov, my hon. friend says-and perhaps this is as good a time as any to refer to the interjection-has it not been shown that in certain respects the Board of Commerce had power beyond the jurisdiction of this House to give? I admit that, and ask hon. gentlemen to reflect that the late government accused, for campaign purposes, of course, of being the ally of the interests and big business, in its legislation did not content itself with mere power of repetitive inquiry; it gave the board power to act, and gave it power even beyond the power of this parliament to give. That was our offence, if offence

there was. But let us see just what was the effect of the Privy Council judgment. The Privy Council judgment, and I do not know that I am particularly competent to define its limits before this House-I will give it in my own words as I understand it-the Privy Council judgment really does not assail or impugn Part One of the Combines and Fair Prices Act. The Privy Council judgment in so far as it impugned the legislation aside from its criminal provisions stated that this parliament had not power to erect a board which would make regulations affecting trade and commerce merely locally, thereby invading the sphere of civil rights. In a word, when we are making regulations as to trade and commerce they must be general regulations, and any board we erect can only enact general regulations affecting the trade and commerce of the whole federal country. We cannot go into the milk business of a town. We cannot go into this special trade and apply regulations there which are really an invasion of civil rights. The Privy Council said more. It said: While you are doing that, getting into civil rights under the guise of trade and commerce law, while you are doing that you cannot validate your legislation by merely declaring that to violate your legislation is a crime. When you are in a sphere in which you should not be, you cannot make yourself right by declaring an offence against your legislation to be a crime. You canot use your criminal jurisdiction as a mere ancillary of what otherwise would be ultra vires legislation. So far the Privy Council went and no further.
Now I venture to suggest this: Within the limits of the Privy Council decision there is nothing at all to prevent the enactment of general regulations by this House or by any board created by this House affecting trade and commerce, and there is nothing to prevent the declaring anything to be a crime under our Criminal Code so long as we do not do it merely to establish the validity of some other legislation which really affects civil rights or invades some other sphere which we have no right to enter. Very well. I only observe this in conclusion on the constitutional phase, lu so far as this legislation makes something a crime which is defined here-I lefer now to section 26-it is at least very doubtful to my mind, and I say it with all deference to the Deputy Minister of Justice, whose opinion I .would like to have read, it is very doubtful to my mind if that clause is within our constitutional powers; but I do not purpose to argue the point.
I want to argue this for the moment. We must have criminal legislation. We must

Combines

Mr. Meighen

protect our rights to enact effective criminal legislation. I am glad to know that that right has not been in any way overthrown by the judgment of the court of appeal in Ontario in the Wholesale Grocers' case. I find on reading the judgment that it has not been. We must preserve our right to enact effective criminal legislation. Our section 498 is good legislation. Perhaps it can be improved. I venture to give this as my opinion: There is no use going any further unless after you have got your board you are going to give that board power to enforce its findings. If you attempt to go further than criminal legislation, by erecting boards to inquire into this, that and the other thing, you are only placing a sham before the people of this country unless you are prepared to go on and give that board power to enforce by general regulation of trade and commerce its own findings as a result of its investigations. This is exactly what this bill does not do. It pretends to go farther, but it only gets into investigation and inquiry, and when it is through with that it is nowhere. The board has no power to make good its findings, no power to enforce its rulings, to deny practices or to compel practices. In a word, it has no executive power at all. When the investigation is through the whole thing is through, and all that it can do is to expose the facts to the attorney general. All this might have been done under the Inquiries Act if such were worth while. But I venture to say again the Criminal Code provisions will be more practically useful left alone. Improve them if you will; make them wider if you will, but leave them there as Criminal Code provisions. Do not provide for an array of official and for mere investigation. The code will be more useful as it is than supplemented by an investigation. Why do I say that? Because I believe an investigation that has no punishment attached to it, no orders that can be enforced, instead of being a deterrent is really a buffer between the offender and punishment. It really gives a man a second chance. It gives him all the case of the prosecution, and thereby enables him to prepare his defence against the time when he gets into a court before which he may be punished. If I were the worst criminal in the country I would not want anything better than to have an investigation first, with all the cards of the prosecution on the table, and then to be given my chance before an effective tribunal after. I would think the criminal far more likely to be punished if the prosecution had the same rights as he and all went to the criminal courts together. That would
!Mr. Meighen.]
be more likely to lead to effective punishment. It is more likely at least, that there would be a verdict of guilty.
In the United Shoe Machinery case I venture to say that if an indictment had been laid under the code in the first place there would have been infinitely greater chance of success than there was after all this circuitous investigation followed by an indictment later on. The United Shoe Machinery Company were made aware of all that was complained about, of all the arguments of the prosecution. They were made aware of everything they had not to do if they wanted to avoid prosecution, and all they had to do was to make this little [DOT] change or that and all would be right. It will be the same under this bili. We will have investigations; we will have all sorts of vexatious inquiries. We will have burdens and expense put on business, but we will not have any real restraint. Wc will not have any effective curtailment of what are declared to be practices to the detriment of the public interest.
I want to try to make a little clear something that I was arguing a moment ago. I put it this way: I do not believe that this definition of a combine, as contained in section 2, is of any value whatever to the purposes of a real prosecution afterwards. It is of value if you have a board which has power to declare what is right and what is wrong and to prevent what is wrong being done. If you have that it is all right. Now let us see. This definition of a combine admits that combines may be good and they may be bad.
A bad combine, it says, is one which operates against the public interest. Very well. A ' board investigates and finds that such and such a practice is against the public interest and therefore it is a bad combine. All well and good. If that board then has power to say "You cannot do that any longer" well and good. The old act said that; the Combines and Fair Prices Act said that; and the board said to the company "You cannot do it any longer" and if the company did it again then it was a crime per se; it was a crime to disobey the orders of the board.
Now, I come to apply this definition to this legislation. The definition, let me repeat, says: "A combine is a combine by business interests that works to the detriment of the public" and it adds "to consumers, to producers and others." It is a combine that works to the detriment of the public and it is undertaken to find out whether such is the case or not. Wherever a registrar finds out that it is he so reports to the

Combines-Mr. Meighen
minister. The minister agrees and then what happens? The matter then goes, or may go, to the criminal court; it canot go anywhere else, the registrar not having the power to stop it or make an issue of the case at all. If it is his opinion that this is a combine which works to the detriment of the public the case goes before the court. The court does not follow the opinion of the minister or the registrar, not at all. You must then convince the court that this is a combine which works to the detriment of the public. The fact that the minister and the registrar have been convinced does not get you anywhere at all. It may be their opinion; it may not be the opinion of the judge, and if it is not, not only has the prior investigation resulted in nothing but even if all the facts disclosed were correct the whole thing is a futility.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend say that if the commissioner has reported that the combination, for example, has been taking advantage of the tariff that the Governor in Council may not then proceed either to reduce the tariff or eliminate it altogether?

I am very glad the Prime Minister mentions that. I intend to refer to it but I do not want to get away from the point I am at until it is clear. The bill as brought down said that a combination was something that was detrimental to the public in the opinion of the registrar. Those words are now omitted. I do not see that it makes much difference because what is left in the bill really amounts to the same effect anyway. The registrar if convinced that there is a combine which is detrimental to the public will report to the minister. Presumably the minister will be convinced of the fact as well, and they expose the facts, we will say, to the attorney general. The very same facts come before the court and the judge does not need to be affected in the least by the opinion of the minister or the opinion of the registrar. He may feel that that combination is not detrimental to the public, and consequently, even though all the facts are correct and even though the company goes there and admits the whole thing, there will not necessarily be any conviction at all. There is just as likely to be a conviction if there had been no investigation whatever. I think there was a greater likelihood of a conviction because the accused person would not have the advantage of knowing the whole case of the prosecution in advance. Consequently an analysis of the proposed legislation convinces me that it is futile and a sham, as such legislation necess-1631
arily is, unless it empowers the registrar, the board, or whatever authority you may provide, to determine what is right and what is wrong, and to prevent what is wrong and to order what is right.
Now the Prime Minister says "Yes, but here is a clause that gives the Governor in Council power to wipe away the protective tariff, to wipe away the duty that protects the industry." He might have added "Here is another clause that gives it power to cancel a patent." But these are all in the statutes now, perhaps not worded exactly the same but the wording can be changed. One is in the Tariff Act. The other is in the Patent Act or in the Tariff Act. The government could have acted upon those. For that matter it is in the< Combines and Fair Prices xlct which is the law of the land to-day; we do not need a new statute to put that clause through. Competent legislation already exists in the Combines and Fair Prices Act which is the law of the land to-day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is declared ultra vires.

Not that section-and in the Tariff Act. You do not need all this preliminary investigation travelling over territory again and again. Let me repeat: All this legislation is simply running in a circle. It is another circle you have to go round; it is just another stump round which you can chase the flat-footed fiend of monopoly. It is nothing more and nothing less.
The Prime Minister argued, both in introducing the resolution and in his speech on the second reading to-day, that now the criminal code provisions cannot be put into effect because the Board of Commerce Act-I think it was the Combines and Fair Prices Act though -says there shall be no prosecution under the code save with the consent of the Board of Commerce. He says there is no Board of Commerce, consequently there can be no prosecution. In that he is right. But you do not need all this machinery to get over that difficulty. If he does not like the Board of Commerce Act let him repeal it. Repeal the Board of Commerce Act, then the code is there clear and in full effect. Also the Prime Minister has his tariff clause, his patent clause; he has everything except this cumbersome machinery expensive to business, provocative to business, burdensome to business, harassing and vexatious. He has everything except some worthless machinery and the power to appoint a whole army of officers the exercise of which can only have one result, namely, to reward the faithful of his party.

Combines-Mr. Murdock
Now, I suggest that the Prime Minister may strengthen his criminal code provisions if he desires. It is quite possible-indeed I think it is likely-that the experience of the years would enable us now to make wider and better the provisions in the criminal code. I think in the criminal code we ought to say what is wrong and what is right. Let us make a clear definition so that men will know what is wrong and what is right, because unless we do we really do not get the effective results. Having done that take ample power to throw off the duties, take ample power to cancel patents; and when the Prime Minister has that, he has everything that is required. If he feels that he ought to go further there is only one way of doing so, there is only one way that is of any value, and that is to give to the board that makes inquiry power to give effect to the findings. If the Prime Minister does that he will really be giving teeth to his legislation. I am not urging him to do it. I do not want to be misunderstood at all-I am disposed to believe that in the present state of business in this country there is no immediate need of	a drastic provision	of that
kind-but unless he does that his legislation is a sham, it is simply circuitous circumlocution, and is a positive burden and expense to business. Consequently, I do not feel that I need bow before the principle of this legislation. Its principle is simply to erect offices and to appoint officers to fill them, but to end up with the supposed culprit given a second chance, a better chance than he would have had if there had not been this legislation.

I am under some obligation to the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) who appeared anxious this afternoon to ascertain where the Minister of Labour stood in regard to this particular legislation. I think therefore it would be entirely improper if I did not allow my position to be known. I think also that my position in regard to this particular legislation should be known, from the fact that my hon. friend for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) seemed to refer Bomewhat disparagingly to the intent underlying this particular bill which is now before the House, and he seemed, as I understood, to imply that if the House could not, in accordance with his views, deal directly and entirely with the cause that they should not undertake in any way to deal with or regulate the effect. That was the understanding which I gathered from my hon. friend's remarks. For the information of my hon. friend for York-

Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) may I say that eome three years ago I intimated where I stood in regard to combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers detrimental to the interest of the public in Canada. I said:
Business men living under the protection of the tariff have got to know each other so well that price fixing agreements, and all sorts of agreements and arrangements, are the rule rather than the exception.
Not all of these are reasonable or proper
The public, unorganized as the sands by the sea, requires a protector against the super-organization of modem business.
I stand here to-night to gladly re-affirm my continued belief in that declaration, and to indicate to my hon. friend for York-Sunbury and others who are inquiring that I stand exactly in the same position to-day as to what should be done in regard to unfair combines, monopolies, trusts or mergers. I would not, however, Mr. Speaker, have one hon. member in this House draw the conclusion from anything I might say that all combines, all so-called monopolies, all price fixing arrangements, and all re-sale price arrangements are detrimental to the interests of the public. I do not believe any such thing. I have not believed that was the case, and. believing as I do, I regard this legislation as drafted generally, with some slight amendments that were suggested by the Prime Minister to-day, as legislation that will not and should not in any way embarrass any business, any combination or any resale price arrangement that is in the interest of the public. But I think, on the other hand, that any combinations, or price fixing arrangements or monopolies that are not working in the public interests know it full well to start with. My experience, if it has been worth anything to me in matters of this kind, is that they know full well that they are exacting the pound of flesh and that they are going beyond reasonable limits in certain cases in exacting unfair prices, or in imposing unfair arrangements on the people of this country. My hon. friend for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), in his opening remarks, referred to the fact that he was not a lawyer, and that therefore he could not deal with this legislation or with combines legislation as a lawyer. He indicated to the House that he was an accountant, and as such would deal with this legislation. Well, I will crave the same privilege by dealing with this legislation as a brake-man, with some knowledge of what the people of Canada desire and demand in respect to a discontinuance of some of the combines that have throttled the prosperity and advance-

Combines-Mr. Murdock
ment of Canada generally in the years gone by, and that may be in evidence at this present moment.
What are they?
