That would appear to be a consistent thing for some one properly authorized under the law to investigate and determine, without either my hon iriend who
inquires "what are they," or myself passing a snap judgment.
May I ask the minister if it is the case that he does not know a single instance of a combine in Canada today that ought to be repressed by law? Will he take that position?

My firm and positive conviction is that there are several combines
in Canada to-day that should be regulated.
Will he name them?
The sugar combine.
I am not at present .sufficiently familiar with the sugar question to advise.
What about Dominion Textile?

My hon. friend for
Vancouver Centre started in on section 2, of the proposed bill No. 54, and expressed great surprise and interest, as to what the words "or others" meant. He appeared to argue-* and I think other hon. members have also argued since-that surely the words "consumers and producers" were sufficient, and that the words "or others" were not necessary. It may be of interest to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre to know that those words are copied identically from the act of 1919 which was passed and placed upon the statute book of Canada by him and his associates when they were in power, and it appeared at that time to be necessary that this language should be used-
The expression "combine" is used in this act with intended relation to articles of commerce, and it shall be deemed to have reference only to such combines immediately hereinafter defined, as, with relation as aforesaid, have in the opinion of the Board of Commerce of Canada
operated, or are likely to operate, to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, consumers, producers or others.
Now, the Combines Act of 1910 did not contain that provision, but in 1919 the government in power, when they were placing on the statute book a law that was heralded broadcast from the Atlantic to the Pacific coast as the last word in protection for the consuming
public of Canada, proceeded to place in that section the words "or others," and let me, as one lay gentleman to another, give my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre my version of why those words "or others" are there. It came to my attention some two or three years ago that these words "or others" were very necessary on account of the business in which such "combinesters" were engaged, that if those words "or others" were not there, they would be able, with legal advice, to prove conclusively that they were neither a producer of the thing they were combined to deal in, nor a consumer of that particular thing, and that therefore, the words "or others" were necessary there to include them and every citizen of this Dominion. That is the view of one layman to another in answer to the question of my hon. friend.
I never asked any such question, and I never argued along the line my hon. friend is arguing. He apparently did not listen to my argument at all.
In order to make a firm punishable, or the members of a combine punishable, who is to decide that their conduct is detrimental to the interest of the public?

The court, and I am coming to that if my right hon. friend can

Combines-Mr. Murdock
possess his soul in patience for only a few minutes.
What does this bill do to hasten the prosecution?
I am coming to that if-
The minister is right at it.
If my right hon. friend can give me only a little time, I will try to get to that in fair order.
The minister is at it now.

I am not in great disagreement with the underlying cause, as defined or suggested by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans), of the things to deal with which we are now here to determine ways and means. I am not in any particular disagreement with him as to what is causing, or what has in a large measure caused some of the things that we are endeavouring, if we can, to provide ways and means to remedy but I must entirely disagree with the thought that it is not proper, because we cannot go right to the root and at the moment do away with the underlying cause, that we should take any steps whatsoever to minimize the effect that is ever present with us to some extent throughout the length and breadth of Canada. There are in effect in Canada to-day conditions that we must for the time being deal with and make provision to deal with, and I now come to what some of my hon. friends have referred to as the "wooden gun" legislation that has been on the statute books of Canada in this respect for some time past. Hon. gentlemen opposite, not only one, but I think, several especially commencing with the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) laid stress upon the fact that the Criminal Code was amply sufficient to protect consumers and producers from all the ills that might come from the formation of an improper combine. My hon. friend must surely know that the Criminal Code is not ready for use to the hand of any consumer or producer in Canada, and it has not been so during the past two or three years.
Will my hon. friend permit me to correct him? I did say that; but I added with the addition of necessary amendments. I pointed that out very distinctly and I think my hon. friend will admit that.

I accept my hon. friend's statement, although I took down right, as I thought, from his lips, the words "legisla-
TMr. Murdock.]
tion unnecessary as Criminal Code sufficient". I now understand that he meant that the Criminal Code would be sufficient when it was fixed up and put into shape, and when the Board of Commerce Act and the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919 were, to all intents and purposes, repealed. My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) shakes his head. The word "repeal" from a layman is wrong. They did not repeal section 498 of the Criminal Code, but they made it impossible for any citizen of Canada to utilize section 498 of the Criminal Code against any combine, monopoly, trust or merger in Canada. My right hon. friend will, of course, say that there is still the Inquiries Act.
I say that all the government has to do, if it does not like the Combines and Fair Prices Act, is to repeal it, and then the Criminal Code is restored in all its^ original force.

I realize, if we can only clear away the driftwood that has been obstructing the vision of the consuming public for the last two or three yean, we shall be able to get something that will put fear into the minds of these combines and monopolies.

The hon. member has said many a time that the Board of Commerce Act and the Combines and Fair Prices Act constituted a "wooden gun " against monopolies. Will he cite a single new power that the registrars or commissioners are to have under this bill that the old Board of Commerce did not have? He knows that the old board had powers that the registrars and commissioners do not have. Will he mention one power that the Board of Commerce did not have, that the registrars are going to have.

The laughable farce or misfortune of the old Board of Commerce Act was the fact that the Board of Commerce had ostensibly entirely too much power. That was the trouble, a power that citizens of Canada high and low could not see the consistency of giving to any board. What power? Power to make an inquiry, power to order an investigation, power to determine guilt, and power up until the time that the criminal was sent along branded to the judge to be sentenced. Entirely improper. The people of Canada very naturally, I think, rebelled at it. Surely it would have been amply sufficient, as contemplated by the measure now under discussion, if that Board of Commerce or another board had had authority to investigate, to look into thj

Combines-Mr. Murdock
allegations that were made against some combine or price-fixing or resale agreement and to determine whether in its opinion such alleged monopoly or agreement was of substantial and material benefit to the consuming and the producing public; or if it was against their interests; and if found to be the latter to refer the case to a court of competent jurisdiction, such as we have throughout the length and breadth of Canada, to adjudicate and assess the guilt and penalty. That as I see it, and, speaking only as a layman, was the great mistake of the Board of Commerce legislation.
Does that not mean that instead of the Board of Commerce being a wooden gun it was a machine gun that shot too often.
It kicked oftener than it shot.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, my right hon. friend is correct in that statement -that is just what would have happened had it not been arranged otherwise.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me what the arrangement was and who it was with? I am asking him to establish it.
You are asking too many questions altogether.
I have been intimating to my right hon. friend for the last three years that I would be only too happy to get into the business of establishing some of that.
Now is your chance. Start right at it.
Bravado at this late date, though, does not change the circumstances of what happened in 1920.

What I understand by bravado is the saying of something of which the hon. gentleman has no proof. I ask him now to establish his proof. I ask him especially to appoint a Board of Inquiry under the Inquiries Act. He is a member of the government now.
Another commission.
Appoint a commissioner' to go into the facts.
Oh, oh.
They laugh. Their colleague alleged-
Order.
He alleged that the members of the then government were holding his hand.
Order.
He is in office to-day-
Order.
You do not like it. He is in office to-day and I ask him to establish his allegation.
I did not allege; I stated.
Now make it good.
I intimated then that I would be glad indeed to undertake to show what was and what was not done.
Now is the time.
Order.
Now, Mr. Speaker-
Oh, oh.
You are not getting on very fast.
Now, Mr. Speaker,while my right hon. friend dealt with the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919 to some extent, I think it should be dealt with more specifically in order to show just-
Just what?

-in order to show that we have not had in Canada, as alleged repeatedly in the late campaign and at various other times, any legislation on the statute books since the Board of Commerce was annulled to deal with a combine, a monopoly or anything of the kind, nothing that a common man could take advantage of, that the plain people-shall I say to use a term favoured by some of my hon. friends?- that the plain people could take advantage of, and now at this particular time when we ask for the enactment of bill No. 54, which provides for the appointment of a registrar whose duty it will be 1;o receive any complaints that are made by the plain people or by the other people of Canada against so-called combines, monopolies, trusts or mergers, we are told by my right hon. friend and his colleagues to go ahead and put some shims under the Criminal Code and fix it up so as to make it fill all necessary purposes. In effect, to you, Mr. Little Retail Grocer, or you Mr. Section Man, or you Mr. Brakeman, or you Mr. Logger in some part of Canada, what does that mean? It means making an
Combines-Mr. Murdock

expensive and cumbersome arrangement hidden in the criminal code that will prevent you in a hundred years, unless you are more financially successful than you have been, from getting into court to prosecute a combine, monopoly, trust or merger, from getting anywhere or receiving any consideration in regard to the things that you allege against some concern that is working detriment to you and the other people of Canada. That is what my hon. friend and some of his associates want to perpetuate, an arrangement in the criminal code that cannot be taken advantage of by the ordinary man, that is available for the big interests, for the wealthy at least as they desire, but that will mean nothing, because too expensive, to the ordinary citizens of Canada, whether producers or consumers.

What does the hon.
gentleman really mean by that anyway? The criminal code is invocable-
Order.

Will hon. gentlemen not permit a correction? The criminal code is invocable by merely laying information, and it is the duty of the attorney general to prosecute. That does not cost the informant anything. This is very expensive to him; the other costs him nothing if the attorney general does his duty.

Mr. Speaker, I quite realize that what my right hon. friend states is what should be; but unfortunately I declare that it is not what is in effect, and I think my right hon. friend knows, and outside of this House would agree, how impossible it would be for some individual- yes, or for six individuals, to get consideration of any suit that they might undertake to institute against some alleged combine, monopoly, trust or merger.
Does the hon. gentleman know an instance-
Order.
Does the hon. gentleman know an instance of anyone laying a charge under the section of the code where the Attorney General refused to prosecute at the public expense?

To-night I am not criticizing any Attorney General in regard to any particular case. I have not in mind, I may say frankly, any particular case where that developed. I do know, though, as I am sure my right hon. friend knows, that under all too many conditions, the provisions of the Criminal fMr. Murdock.)
Code are not available for the purposes of the representations of the poor man, especially where, banked against the aims and endeavours thus contemplated, are, possibly, great sums of money protecting the concern that it is proposed to prosecute.
Another point that was very much stressed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, the hon. member for Fort William and others was with regard to the one-man representation, which was referred to as unfair and inconsistent. On the opening of this debate to-day the Prime Minister indicated that the one-man arrangement was going to be changed and that an amendment was to be proposed to make it necessary, as in the 1910 act, for six persons to indicate their belief that a combine exists. The act of 1910, which was repealed by the government of my right hon. friend, provided that where six or more persons, British subjects resident in Canada and of full age, were of the opinion that a combine existed, that prices had been enhanced or competition restricted, they might make the necessary representation, But when it came to 1919 and the present leader of the Opposition and his colleagues were fixing up legislation that was to be heralded and broadcasted as the real thing in combine hunting, it was provided in section 6 that any British subject resident in Canada and of full age who was of the opinion that a combine existed or was being formed might apply in writing to any member of the board except the Chief Commissioner for an order, and so on. I want to remind my hon. friends opposite that the safeguard contained in the 1910 statute against the possibility of some individual, for spite or any other reason, making a charge against some concern, was regarded by them as unnecessary; one man was thought sufficient. And now, because in the first text of the bill as brought down one man is specified, my hon. friends lay emphasis on the fact that is in their opinion, improper. I agree that six would be very much better.
One hon. gentleman suggested that the act contemplated the appointment of registrars here and there and everywhere throughout the length and breadth of Canada. Surely the bill must have been hurriedly read if that opinion was gained from it; nothing of the kind is contemplated. The act provides for the appointment of a registrar-one registrar-whose duty will be to receive representations that may be made from time to time indicating the belief of certain individuals that a combine, a monopoly, a resale price fixing arrangement is in effect or about to be put into effect. And when the registrar re-

Combines-Mr. Murdock
ceives a complaint of that kind, it is his duty so to proceed as to demoralize and disorganize business? Not by any means. He will read what is conveyed to him as the view of those making the representations, and then, in a quiet and orderly way, he will make inquiries to ascertain what are the actual facts. We have had in Canada since 1906 a registrar of boards of conciliation and investigation under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. That registrar does not authorize the formation of a board in the case of every application made therefor. It has been found in something more than one hundred cases since the passing of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act that the application for a board was based on an improper understanding or ill-founded claim on the part of the applicants, and they have been so advised. The public very seldom know anything about these decisions of the registrar; the correspondence is usually conducted between the parties making the application and the registrar. The registrar, at least at times, consults with the minister to ascertain his view or the view of the government in the matter. In Bill No. 54 exactly the same function is proposed in the appointment of one registrar located in or close to the office of the minister, where he will receive complaints that are made, analyze them and determine whether there is anything in them. He can go to the extent of asking for documents, requesting information, quietly investigating without any thought or intention or desire to disrupt or disorganize business, but only with the view of ascertaining the actual conditions in connection with the business in question, to secure such information for the purpose of conveying it to those who have complained that an improper condition exists. What is fairer than that? What can be more regular or orderly in the matter of stabilizing any legitimate business that is liable to have the charge hurled against it that it is a combine or monopoly and that its operations in that respect are detrimental to the public? Then, if the registrar believes after quiet inquiry that some things in the complaint are not satisfactorily answered, the act provides that a commissioner can be appointed-presumably someone amply qualified to analyze and investigate thoroughly, in fact, to understand, the particular business or concern that is to be investigated-a commissioner presumably amply qualified to deal with the subject that is to be brought under investigation. The commissioner proceeds to that investigation. He takes such means as the act provides to bring out all the facts which the producers and consumers of Canada are
entitled to ascertain if there is as alleged a combine or any other business arrangement that is detrimental to the consumer and the producer. He brings out all that information and then makes his report.	,
My right hon. friend objects right at that point. After the commissioner has ascertained all that it is possible for the lay mind to ascertain-because the act does not provide that a lawyer must have the job every time a commissioner is to be appointed, or say that there are not business men throughout the length and breadth of Canada experienced in all lines of industry who may be just as capable of determining business conditions in effect as a lawyer-after the commissioner has analysed from every standpoint the conditions alleged and has decided that there is in his judgment some arrangement in effect that is not in the interest of producers and consumers and has made his report, what more logical arrangement, what more consistent with British justice could be suggested than that the culprit believed to have instituted a combine, monopoly, trust or merger should be brought before a court of competent jurisdiction anywhere throughout the length and breadth of Canada to plead his case, as he would have a right to do, before a jury of his peers? They decide on the facts presented, and then the judge on the bench determines in accordance with the provisions of this act the penalty to be applied if the verdict is guilty. That is where the Board of Commerce Act and the Combines and Fair Prices Act fell down. In the first place it undertook, the way it worked out, to make a judge out of a brakeman without any legal experience, to assess penalties, to define crime and say what should be done. This act proceeds in a more orderly way. It recognizes the courts of competent jurisdiction in Canada to-day, and as quietly and as unobtrusively as possible-I repeat	that-as
quietly and as unobtrusively as possible provides for a preliminary inquiry by the registrar and the commissioner. Why not? Why does some hon. gentleman talk of secret diplomacy and suggest that a secret inquiry should not be made? Is it not reasonable to act on the assumption that the registrar, yea, and the commissioner, when appointed may find that there was nothing sufficiently tangible upon which to base a claim of improper conduct against some particular combine? Why should that particular concern, if things are being done on the level and in the interest of consumer and producer, if fixing resale prices, for instance, in the interest of the consumer, if we want to deal fairly, why should

it be necessary to herald this preliminary investigation from the housetops until the case finally comes to a court of competent jurisdiction for determination? I do not mean, Mr. Speaker, to imply that there will be no notoriety whatsoever before the case gets into court, but I do mean to suggest that to be fair to all concerned there should be as little notoriety as possible given to the preliminary investigation by either registrar or commissioner, for the simple reason that their investigation as contemplated is only preliminary and the concern itself is to have its day in court in the final analysis to show whether it is guilty or innocent of the charge alleged, and which either the registrar or the commissioner may believe. There is no question at all about the final investigation before a court of competent jurisdiction being given sufficient notoriety.
I have, Mr. Speaker, three more pages of references to the remarks of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, and as I do not wish to take up any more time tonight I move the adjournment of the debate.
